# chloro

> A Rust code formatter that reproduces rustfmt's output, byte for byte, without the compiler

chloro is a Rust code formatter that writes the same bytes as rustfmt (1.9.0 by default,
or 1.8.0), several times faster and without the Rust compiler. It is a command-line tool
(`chloro`) and two library crates (`chloro`, `chloro-core`; API on docs.rs). Each link
below is the Markdown version of a page of https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/.

# Start here

# chloro

rustfmt's output in a fraction of the time.

chloro formats Rust several times faster than rustfmt, in a fraction of the memory, and writes the same bytes as `rustfmt --edition 2024`. It is a module-by-module port of rustfmt 1.9.0's formatting code onto the syntax trees of rust-analyzer's parser, so it does not need the Rust compiler. It comes as a 2 MB command-line tool and as a library.

1220/1220 rust-analyzer files formatted identically to rustfmt 1.9.0, and to rustfmt 1.8.0 default options, none non-idempotent; [rustfmt compatibility](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/compatibility/index.md>)

Controlled benchmark

Nine crates vs rustfmt 1.9.0

|  | wall time, speedup | peak memory |
| --- | --- | --- |
| rustfmt | 1× | 43–86 MiB |
| chloro, 1 core | 2.9–4.7× | 4–10 MiB |
| chloro, 4 cores | 6.1–13× | 5–23 MiB |

hir, hir-ty, ide-db, syntax and parser from rust-analyzer, and tokio, regex-syntax, clap\_builder and winnow from crates.io: 215 KB–2.9 MB each. An idle four-core Linux VM, 30 runs per cell, one-core runs pinned. Ranges span the nine crates.

A large real-world workspace

ruff vs `cargo fmt`, rustfmt 1.10.0

|  | wall time, speedup | peak memory |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cargo fmt` | 1× | 194 MiB |
| chloro, 1 thread | 3.5× | 16 MiB |
| chloro, 20 threads | 26.5× | 90 MiB |

The whole [ruff](<https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff>) repository: 2,008 files in one run of each tool, so one figure per row. A 20-core workstation, 5 runs each (`just vs-ruff`).

The speedup is rustfmt's wall time divided by chloro's, checking already-formatted files. rustfmt formats on one thread, so the one-core and one-thread rows compare the two formatters like for like; the last row of each adds chloro's parallelism. Each bar is wall time, the baseline's as the full bar; the nine crates' bars show their spread. The panels compare against different rustfmt releases: 1.9.0, the one chloro reproduces, and 1.10.0, the one ruff's toolchain pins. The method, every workload and the limits of these numbers are on the [Performance](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/performance/index.md>) page.

## Getting started

```sh
cargo binstall chloro          # or: cargo install chloro --features cli
chloro --check src/            # exit 1 if any file would change
chloro --write src/            # format in place
```

```rust
let formatted = chloro::format_source("fn main(){let x=1;}\n");
assert_eq!(formatted, "fn main() {\n    let x = 1;\n}\n");
```

## Compatibility with rustfmt

chloro's formatting modules follow rustfmt's source files (`items`, `expr`, `chains`, `lists`, `comment` and so on), so each formatting decision can be checked against the rustfmt code it comes from. Any output that differs from rustfmt's is a bug; the [known differences](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/compatibility/#known-differences>) are listed.

It takes rustfmt's stable options under their rustfmt names (`max_width`, `tab_spaces`, `use_small_heuristics`, `edition`, `style_edition` and the rest), either as `--config key=value` on the command line or on a `Config` in the library. Unstable options keep their default values. By default it reproduces rustfmt 1.9.0; with `rustfmt_version = "1.8.0"` it reproduces rustfmt 1.8.0, the release shipped with Rust 1.88.

The command line is not a replacement for the `rustfmt` binary: chloro does not read `rustfmt.toml`, has no `--emit` modes, and does not format standard input. [rustfmt compatibility](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/compatibility/#what-is-not-covered>) lists the other differences.

## Documentation

[**Install**Pre-built binaries, building from source, and the two crates.](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/getting-started/installation/index.md>) [**Quickstart**Check a project, format it, and use it in CI.](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/getting-started/quickstart/index.md>) [**Command line**Sources, modes, exit codes, options, threads and caches.](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/cli/index.md>) [**Library**Format strings from Rust, in parallel or with a cache of items.](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/library/index.md>) [**rustfmt compatibility**What is compared, against which rustfmt, and what is known to differ.](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/compatibility/index.md>) [**How it works**From source text to rustfmt's bytes: lexer, flat syntax tree, ported formatter.](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/architecture/overview/index.md>)

chloro is open source under MIT or Apache-2.0, at [github.com/lmmx/chloro](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro>). The Rust API is documented on [docs.rs/chloro](<https://docs.rs/chloro>) and [docs.rs/chloro-core](<https://docs.rs/chloro-core>).

# Installation

chloro is published as two crates: `chloro`, which holds the command-line tool and a small library facade, and `chloro-core`, the formatter itself.

## The command-line tool

```sh
cargo binstall chloro
```

[cargo-binstall](<https://github.com/cargo-bins/cargo-binstall>) downloads the binary attached to the [GitHub release](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/releases>) for your platform. Releases have binaries for `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` and `aarch64-pc-windows-msvc`, and for macOS where its runner built them (the [release page](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/releases>) lists them); on any other platform `cargo binstall` falls back to building from source.

```sh
cargo install chloro --features cli
```

The binary is behind the `cli` feature, so that a library dependency on `chloro` does not pull in the command line's dependencies. Building needs Rust 1.88 or later (the workspace's `rust-version`).

```sh
git clone https://github.com/lmmx/chloro
cd chloro
cargo install --path chloro --features cli
```

Check that it runs:

```sh
chloro --help
```

The release profile builds with fat link-time optimisation and one codegen unit, which makes a from-source build slower than a default release build. Release binaries for the targets that GitHub's runners execute natively can also be built with profile-guided optimisation; see [Releasing](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/maintainers/releasing/#profile-guided-builds>).

## The library

Add `chloro` to your `Cargo.toml` for the formatting functions and `Config`:

```toml
[dependencies]
chloro = "0.9"
```

`chloro` re-exports `format_source`, `format_source_with_config` and `Config` from `chloro-core`. The parallel and cached entry points, and the syntax tree, are only in `chloro-core`:

```toml
[dependencies]
chloro-core = "0.9"
```

Both crates have no default features. The [Library guide](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/library/index.md>) shows what each entry point does, and the [Rust API reference](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/reference/api/index.md>) lists them with links to docs.rs.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Versions**
>
> This site describes chloro 0.9.0. The [Changelog](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/changelog/index.md>) says which version each change is in, and `chloro --version` which version you have.

## Run-time requirements

chloro has no run-time dependencies. It does not call `rustfmt`, `rustc` or `cargo`, and it reads no configuration file: options come from `--config` on the command line or from `Config` in the library. Apart from the files it formats, the only file it writes is its [cache](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/caching/index.md>), which lives in the user cache directory by default.

# Quickstart

How to check and format a crate with chloro, and how to run the check in CI. Each command gives the same result as `rustfmt` at edition 2024 with default options.

## Check

From the root of a crate:

```console
$ chloro --check src/ tests/ examples/

Error: 3 file(s) need formatting
```

`--check` formats every `.rs` file under the paths you name, writes nothing, and exits with status 1 if any file's formatted text differs from what is on disk. Every path must exist: a missing one is an error before anything is formatted. Add `--verbose` to see each file as it is processed and a summary at the end.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Which files**
>
> chloro walks the directories under the paths it is given for `.rs` files, skipping hidden entries (names starting with `.`, such as `.git`) and cache directories such as Cargo's `target/`. It does not read `.gitignore`. With no path it starts at the current directory, so `chloro --check` at the root of a Cargo project checks the project's sources ([Sources](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/cli/#sources>)).

## Format

```sh
chloro --write src/ tests/ examples/
```

`--write` rewrites each file whose formatted text differs, and leaves the others untouched. Without `--check` or `--write`, chloro prints each formatted file to standard output, which is useful for a single file:

```sh
chloro src/lib.rs | diff src/lib.rs -
```

## Choose options

chloro takes rustfmt's stable options by rustfmt's names, as comma-separated `key=value` pairs:

```sh
chloro --config max_width=80,tab_spaces=2 --write src/
chloro --config edition=2021 --check src/
chloro --config rustfmt_version=1.8.0 --check src/
```

An unknown option, a malformed value or an unstable rustfmt option set away from its default stops the run before any file is read:

```console
$ chloro --config wrap_comments=true src/
Error: invalid --config: `wrap_comments` is an unstable rustfmt option; only its default `false` is supported
```

chloro does not read `rustfmt.toml`. If your project has one, translate its stable options into `--config`; [Configuration](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/configuration/index.md>) lists every option chloro accepts.

## Use it in CI

A GitHub Actions job that fails when a file is not formatted:

```yaml
jobs:
  format:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: taiki-e/install-action@v2
        with:
          tool: cargo-binstall
      - run: cargo binstall --no-confirm chloro
      - run: chloro --check --no-cache src/ tests/
```

`--no-cache` is optional. A CI runner starts with an empty cache, so the cache has nothing to answer from; in the measurements a cold cache cost 364 ms against 356 ms without one on a 1238-file tree (see [Caching](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/caching/index.md>)).

## Call it from Rust

```rust
let mut config = chloro::Config::default();
config.set("max_width", "80").unwrap();
let formatted = chloro::format_source_with_config("fn main(){let x=1;}", &config);
assert_eq!(formatted, "fn main() {\n    let x = 1;\n}\n");
```

The [Library guide](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/library/index.md>) covers the rest of the API, including formatting one large file on several threads.

# Guide

# Command line

chloro formats the `.rs` files under the paths you give it. Depending on the flags, it prints the formatted files, checks them against what is on disk, or writes them back.

```text
chloro [OPTIONS] [SOURCES]...
```

## Sources

Each source is a file or a directory. A directory is walked recursively for files ending in `.rs`; a file named directly is formatted whatever its extension. With no source, chloro starts at the current directory.

- The walk skips hidden entries, whose names start with `.` (`.git/`, `.cargo/`, `.hidden.rs`), and cache directories: a directory with a `CACHEDIR.TAG` file, as Cargo writes in every `target/` directory (the [Cache Directory Tagging Specification](<https://bford.info/cachedir/>)). So `chloro --check` at the root of a Cargo project checks its sources and not its build output.
- A source named on the command line is always used, hidden or tagged: `chloro target/` walks `target/`, and `chloro .hidden.rs` formats that file.
- `.gitignore` is not read.
- A file reachable twice (named twice, reached through a symlink, or both named and found in a directory) is formatted once.
- A symlinked directory that points back into a directory being walked is not followed again.
- A source path that does not exist is an error, reported before any file is formatted.

## Modes

**<kbd>--check</kbd>**

Format every file and compare. Nothing is written. Exits with status 1 and `Error: N file(s) need formatting` when at least one file would change.

**<kbd>--write</kbd>**

Write each file whose formatted text differs from its contents. Files that are already formatted are not touched.

**(neither)**

Print every formatted file to standard output, one after another. With more than one thread, files are printed in the order they finish, which can vary from run to run; use `--threads 1` for a stable order, or name one file.

With both `--check` and `--write`, files are written and the exit status reports whether any needed formatting.

## Exit status

| status | when |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | every file was processed; with `--check`, none needs formatting |
| 1 | `--check` found files that need formatting; or a file does not parse; or a file could not be read or written; or a source path does not exist; or `--config` was invalid; or the arguments could not be parsed |

A file that does not parse, or that contains syntax rustc's parser rejects, is reported as rustfmt reports it, in every mode: its error is printed to standard error in rustc's layout, nothing is printed or written for it, and the exit status is 1. The other files are formatted as usual.

```text
error: expected expression, found `;`
 --> /home/me/project/src/main.rs:2:13
  |
2 |     let x = ;
  |             ^
```

The position is where rustc reports most syntax errors. The message is rust-analyzer's parser's, worded like rustc's where its tokens allow (as in "expected `;`, found keyword `let`"), or, for syntax that rust-analyzer's parser accepts and rustc's rejects, "rustc's parser rejects this syntax"; rustc's own messages, notes and suggestions are not reproduced. Only the first error of a file is reported. The errors are printed after the run, in path order, `--verbose` counts the files in its summary ("Files that do not parse"), and such a file is never recorded in the cache. A file with an inner `#![rustfmt::skip]` attribute is left unchanged, and is not an error.

## Options

The flags are summarised here; the [CLI reference](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/reference/cli/index.md>) has the full help text.

| option | what it does | guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-c`, `--check` | exit 1 if any file would change; write nothing | [above](<#modes>) |
| `-w`, `--write` | write formatted files in place | [above](<#modes>) |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | report each file, the cache in use, the thread count and a summary, on standard error |  |
| `--config OPTS` | rustfmt options as `key=value,key=value` | [Configuration](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/configuration/index.md>) |
| `--threads N` | worker threads (default: one per core) | [Parallelism](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/parallelism/index.md>) |
| `--no-cache` | neither read nor write the caches | [Caching](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/caching/index.md>) |
| `--unit-cache` | also cache each formatted top-level item | [Caching](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/caching/#the-unit-cache>) |
| `--cache-dir DIR` | where the caches live | [Caching](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/caching/#where-the-cache-lives>) |
| `-V`, `--version` | print the version, marked `-dev` unless built from the release | [Reference](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/reference/cli/#-version-v>) |
| `-h`, `--help` | print the help text |  |

> [!NOTE]
>
> **The default source in `--help`**
>
> The help text describes the default source as `'src'`; the default is in fact the current directory (`.`), as described above ([\#91](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/issues/91>)).

## Environment variables

| variable | effect |
| --- | --- |
| `CHLORO_CACHE_DIR` | the cache directory when `--cache-dir` is not given |
| `XDG_CACHE_HOME` | when set, the default cache directory is `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/chloro` (on every platform) |
| `CHLORO_TRACE=FILE` | write a per-file, per-worker timeline of the run to `FILE` (a diagnostic for [scheduling](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/parallelism/#seeing-the-schedule>)) |

## Byte order marks and line endings

chloro handles both as rustfmt does:

- The file is formatted as rustc reads it: without a byte order mark at the start, and with `\r\n` read as `\n`.
- The output's line endings follow the `newline_style` option. `Unix` and `Windows` force `\n` or `\r\n`, and `Native` uses the platform's. The default, `Auto`, takes the style of the first line ending of the text as rustc reads it, in which `\r\n` is already `\n`: so the output has `\n` line endings (the platform's for a file without a line break).
- Whether a file needs formatting is decided as rustfmt decides it. Under `Auto`, a file that differs from its formatted output only in its `\r\n` line endings or a byte order mark is formatted: `--check` passes and `--write` leaves it as it is. A file with `\r\n` line endings that does need formatting is written with `\n` ones. Under the other styles, any difference in the bytes counts.

A few things rustfmt does that chloro does not (reading `rustfmt.toml`, `--emit`, formatting standard input) are listed under [rustfmt compatibility](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/compatibility/#what-is-not-covered>).

# Configuration

chloro accepts rustfmt's stable options, with the same names, value spellings and defaults. It adds one option, `rustfmt_version`, which selects the rustfmt release to reproduce.

With no options, chloro formats as `rustfmt --edition 2024` does with no `rustfmt.toml`.

## Setting options

```sh
chloro --config max_width=80,use_small_heuristics=Max --write src/
```

`--config` takes comma-separated `key=value` pairs, as rustfmt's `--config` does. Values may be quoted (`edition="2021"`).

```rust
let mut config = chloro::Config::default();
config.set("max_width", "80").unwrap();
config.set("use_small_heuristics", "Max").unwrap();
let formatted = chloro::format_source_with_config("fn main() {}\n", &config);
```

`Config::set` takes the same names and spellings as `--config` and returns an error message for an unknown option or an invalid value.

```rust
let config = chloro::Config {
    max_width: 80,
    tab_spaces: 2,
    ..chloro::Config::default()
};
let formatted = chloro::format_source_with_config("fn main() {}\n", &config);
```

Every stable option is a public field of `Config`. The enum-valued fields (`newline_style`, `edition`, …) take types from `chloro_core::formatter::config`.

chloro does not read `rustfmt.toml` or `.rustfmt.toml`. A project that has one can pass its stable options through `--config`:

rustfmt.toml

```toml
max_width = 120
use_field_init_shorthand = true
```

```sh
chloro --config max_width=120,use_field_init_shorthand=true --check src/
```

## The options

| option | default | values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `max_width` | `100` | unsigned integer |
| `hard_tabs` | `false` | `true`, `false` |
| `tab_spaces` | `4` | unsigned integer |
| `newline_style` | `Auto` | `Auto`, `Native`, `Unix`, `Windows` |
| `use_small_heuristics` | `Default` | `Default`, `Max`, `Off` |
| `fn_call_width` | from `use_small_heuristics` (60) | unsigned integer |
| `attr_fn_like_width` | from `use_small_heuristics` (70) | unsigned integer |
| `struct_lit_width` | from `use_small_heuristics` (18) | unsigned integer |
| `struct_variant_width` | from `use_small_heuristics` (35) | unsigned integer |
| `array_width` | from `use_small_heuristics` (60) | unsigned integer |
| `chain_width` | from `use_small_heuristics` (60) | unsigned integer |
| `single_line_if_else_max_width` | from `use_small_heuristics` (50) | unsigned integer; `0` always breaks |
| `single_line_let_else_max_width` | from `use_small_heuristics` (50) | unsigned integer; `0` always breaks |
| `reorder_imports` | `true` | `true`, `false` |
| `reorder_modules` | `true` | `true`, `false` |
| `remove_nested_parens` | `true` | `true`, `false` |
| `short_array_element_width_threshold` | `10` | unsigned integer |
| `match_arm_leading_pipes` | `Never` | `Always`, `Never`, `Preserve` |
| `fn_params_layout` (or `fn_args_layout`) | `Tall` | `Compressed`, `Tall`, `Vertical` |
| `match_block_trailing_comma` | `false` | `true`, `false` |
| `edition` | `2024` | `2015`, `2018`, `2021`, `2024` |
| `style_edition` | follows `edition` | `2015`, `2018`, `2021`, `2024` |
| `merge_derives` | `true` | `true`, `false` |
| `use_try_shorthand` | `false` | `true`, `false` |
| `use_field_init_shorthand` | `false` | `true`, `false` |
| `force_explicit_abi` | `true` | `true`, `false` |
| `disable_all_formatting` | `false` | `true`, `false` |
| `rustfmt_version` | `1.9.0` | `1.8.0`, `1.9.0` (chloro only) |

Each option means what it means in rustfmt; the [rustfmt configuration reference](<https://rust-lang.github.io/rustfmt/>) describes them. [rustfmt compatibility](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/compatibility/#options>) lists the option values on which chloro's output has been compared with rustfmt's.

### Width heuristics

The eight width options, `fn_call_width` to `single_line_let_else_max_width`, are derived from `max_width` unless set, as in rustfmt:

- `use_small_heuristics = Default` uses the values in brackets above at `max_width = 100`, scaled by `max_width / 100` (rounded to the nearest tenth) when `max_width` is larger.
- `Max` sets each to `max_width`.
- `Off` sets each to 0.

An explicitly set width wins over the heuristic and is capped at `max_width`.

### Editions

`edition` is the Rust edition the source is parsed as: it decides what is a keyword and what syntax is accepted. `style_edition` is the edition of the Rust Style Guide the output follows. As in rustfmt, an unset `style_edition` follows `edition`, so `edition=2021` alone formats with the 2021 style. Style editions 2015, 2018 and 2021 are the same style; 2024 differs from them.

### `rustfmt_version`

This option is specific to chloro. It selects the rustfmt release whose output is reproduced:

- `1.9.0`, the default: `rustfmt 1.9.0-stable (2d8144b788 2026-07-07)`, the release chloro is ported from.
- `1.8.0`: `rustfmt 1.8.0-stable (6b00bc3880 2025-06-23)`, as shipped with Rust 1.88.0.

The two releases differ in a handful of formatting decisions and in which syntax their parsers accept; [rustfmt compatibility](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/compatibility/#rustfmt-releases>) lists the differences. `1.7.0` and earlier are rejected with an explanation: rustfmt 1.7.0 has no 2024 Style Guide rules, and its output differs from 1.9.0's too widely to reproduce with a few version checks in the formatter.

### Unstable rustfmt options

rustfmt's unstable options (those that need nightly rustfmt) are not configurable. chloro always behaves as rustfmt does with each at its default. Naming one with its default value is accepted, so a configuration written for stable rustfmt still works; any other value is an error:

```console
$ chloro --config wrap_comments=true src/
Error: invalid --config: `wrap_comments` is an unstable rustfmt option; only its default `false` is supported
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> **The unstable options and the defaults chloro applies**
>
> `indent_style = Block`, `wrap_comments = false`, `format_code_in_doc_comments = false`, `doc_comment_code_block_width = 100`, `comment_width = 80`, `normalize_comments = false`, `normalize_doc_attributes = false`, `format_strings = false`, `format_macro_matchers = false`, `format_macro_bodies = true`, `skip_macro_invocations = []`, `hex_literal_case = Preserve`, `float_literal_trailing_zero = Preserve`, `empty_item_single_line = true`, `struct_lit_single_line = true`, `fn_single_line = false`, `where_single_line = false`, `imports_indent = Block`, `imports_layout = Mixed`, `imports_granularity = Preserve`, `group_imports = Preserve`, `reorder_impl_items = false`, `type_punctuation_density = Wide`, `space_before_colon = false`, `space_after_colon = true`, `spaces_around_ranges = false`, `binop_separator = Front`, `combine_control_expr = true`, `overflow_delimited_expr = false`, `struct_field_align_threshold = 0`, `enum_discrim_align_threshold = 0`, `match_arm_blocks = true`, `match_arm_indent = true`, `force_multiline_blocks = false`, `brace_style = SameLineWhere`, `control_brace_style = AlwaysSameLine`, `trailing_semicolon = true`, `trailing_comma = Vertical`, `blank_lines_upper_bound = 1`, `blank_lines_lower_bound = 0`, `inline_attribute_width = 0`, `format_generated_files = true`, `condense_wildcard_suffixes = false`.

## Attributes in the source

chloro honours rustfmt's attributes:

- `#![rustfmt::skip]` as an inner attribute of a file leaves the file as written.
- `#[rustfmt::skip]` on an item, statement or expression leaves that node as written.
- `#[rustfmt::skip::macros(name, …)]` and `#[rustfmt::skip::attributes(name, …)]` leave calls of those macros, or those attributes, as written inside the item they are on; as inner attributes (`#![…]`) they apply to the whole file or module.

# Parallelism

By default chloro uses every core. Files are spread across worker threads, and a large file has its top-level items formatted on several threads at once. The output is identical whatever the number of threads.

## Files in parallel

The command line starts one worker per core (`std::thread::available_parallelism`), or `--threads N` workers. The files are sorted by size, largest first, and handed out from a shared queue: each worker takes the next file as soon as it finishes one. Starting with the large files keeps one late, large file from leaving the other cores idle at the end of a run.

```sh
chloro --check src/                 # one worker per core
chloro --threads 2 --check src/     # two workers
chloro --threads 1 --check src/     # sequential
```

rustfmt formats the files of a crate on one thread. On the nine crates of the [performance measurements](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/performance/index.md>), chloro on four cores took 0.08–0.17 of rustfmt's wall time, against 0.21–0.35 on one core.

## Large files

A file of 128 KiB or more is also split: its top-level items are formatted on up to `--threads` threads, while the text between the items (comments, blank lines, items left as written) is written in order on one thread and the formatted items are put back between it. The threshold is a constant of the command line (`PARALLEL_ITEMS_MIN_BYTES`); below it, starting threads for one file costs more than it saves when the other cores are already busy with other files.

On the five largest files of the conformance corpus, formatting each file alone with four threads was 1.1–1.7 times as fast as with one, for 1.09–1.32 times the CPU time.

Splitting a file does not change its output, because in rustfmt the output of a top-level item depends only on the item's own text and the configuration. The exceptions are the text between items, and groups of `use`, `mod` and `extern crate` items, which rustfmt sorts together. chloro keeps both on the calling thread and treats a sortable group as a single unit. [Parallelism and caches](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/architecture/concurrency/index.md>) explains how the pieces are put back together and how that is tested.

The library exposes the same split as [`format_source_with_config_parallel`](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/library/#one-large-file-on-several-threads>); the library never starts threads unless asked.

## Output order

With `--check` or `--write` the order in which files finish does not matter. When printing to standard output, each file is written as soon as it is formatted, so with several threads the order of the files can vary between runs (the bytes of each file do not). Use `--threads 1` when the order matters.

## Seeing the schedule

`CHLORO_TRACE=FILE` makes the command line write a timeline of the run: when each worker took each file, and when it read, hashed and formatted it. The scripts under `benchmarks/schedule/` turn a trace into per-worker idle time and the length of the run's tail. On the measured crates the schedule came within 1–1.5% of the shortest possible for the work, so there is little to gain from changing it.

# Caching

Most formatter runs, from a pre-commit hook or an editor on save, are over files that are already formatted. chloro records which file contents it has seen come out unchanged and skips them on later runs.

## The fixed-point cache

When chloro finds a file already formatted, it records the file's BLAKE3 digest. On a later run, a file whose digest is recorded is reported as formatted without being parsed. The digest is recorded only for content observed to be a fixed point: a file left unchanged by the run, or a file just written whose formatted text formats to itself.

The cache is on by default for `--check`, `--write` and printing. It never changes what chloro does: the output and the exit status of a run are the same with and without it.

On the 1238 already-formatted files of the conformance corpus, on four cores:

| run | wall time |
| --- | --- |
| `--check`, warm cache | 16.2 ms |
| `--check`, cache directory removed before the run | 364 ms |
| `--check --no-cache` | 356 ms |
| `--check` with chloro 0.8.0, which has no cache | 1014 ms |

These figures are from measurement [M6](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-14-autoresearch/measurements/m6-quiet-host.md>); the [Performance](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/performance/index.md>) page describes the conditions.

### What the key covers

Each cache file holds the digests for one chloro binary and one configuration:

- **The binary.** The BLAKE3 digest of the running executable, with the crate version, the cache format version and the target. Rebuilding or upgrading chloro starts a new cache file, so a digest recorded by one build is never trusted by another.
- **The configuration.** Every field of the `Config` built from `--config`, serialised field by field. Changing an option starts a new cache file.
- **The content.** The digest of the file's exact bytes. Paths and timestamps of source files are not recorded, so renaming or touching a file does not invalidate it.

Hashing the 2 MB executable on every run would cost more than the rest of a small run, so its digest is recorded under the executable's identity (path, size and modification time, and on Unix also device, inode and status-change time) and read back while that identity is unchanged.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Limitation**
>
> An executable rewritten in place with every one of those identity fields unchanged would be taken for the binary recorded earlier. On Unix that requires a write within the file system's timestamp granularity of the previous change, a clock set back, or a write that bypasses the file system; on Windows, where the identity is path, size and modification time, a same-size rewrite with the modification time restored. Use `--no-cache`, or remove the cache directory, if you replace chloro's binary by such means.

### Where the cache lives

chloro uses the first of these that is set:

1. `--cache-dir DIR`
2. `$CHLORO_CACHE_DIR`
3. `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/chloro`
4. `%LOCALAPPDATA%\chloro\cache` on Windows
5. `~/Library/Caches/chloro` on macOS
6. `~/.cache/chloro`

If none can be resolved, the run proceeds without a cache. `--verbose` prints the cache file in use and how many entries it holds.

The directory holds `*.chloro-cache` files (one per binary and configuration), `*.chloro-exe` records of executable digests and, with `--unit-cache`, `*.chloro-units` files. A cache file keeps at most 131,072 digests, dropping the least recently seen; files not written for 30 days are removed by later runs. Writes go to a temporary file that is renamed into place, so concurrent runs do not corrupt a cache; deleting the directory at any time is safe.

### Turning it off

```sh
chloro --no-cache --check src/
```

`--no-cache` neither reads nor writes any cache, the unit cache included.

## The unit cache

`--unit-cache` adds a second, opt-in cache, for files that did change. It keeps the formatted text of each top-level item (or each group of `use`, `mod` and `extern crate` items that rustfmt sorts together), keyed by the item's text, the whole configuration and the file's `rustfmt::skip` names. When a file changes, only the items not seen before are formatted; the rest of the file (the parse, the checks that apply to the whole file, the text between items) is recomputed every time, so the result is exactly what formatting the whole file gives. This was verified over the conformance corpus and a registry corpus of 25,077 files, at one and four threads.

```sh
chloro --unit-cache --write src/
```

It is off by default because it costs more than it saves when it starts empty: a cold `--check` of the conformance corpus took 10–15% longer with it, and its file grew to 8.6 MB for that corpus. It helps when the same large files are reformatted after small edits. In process, reformatting a large file after a one-item edit took 0.26–0.47 of the time of formatting it from scratch; at the command line, process start-up and reading the cache take back part of that saving. The records are capped at 64 MiB per cache file.

The library exposes the same mechanism, with a store you provide; see [the library guide](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/library/#a-cache-of-formatted-items>).

# Library

Each of chloro's library functions takes source text and returns formatted text. None of them reads or writes files, and none starts a thread unless you ask for threads.

## Which crate

| crate | what it gives you |
| --- | --- |
| [`chloro`](<https://docs.rs/chloro>) | `format_source`, `format_source_with_config`, `try_format_source_with_config`, `Config`, `ParseError`; and the command line behind the `cli` feature |
| [`chloro-core`](<https://docs.rs/chloro-core>) | all of the above, plus the parallel and cached entry points, `parse_only`, and the syntax tree |

`chloro` re-exports these items from `chloro-core`, so both crates use the same `Config` type. The examples on this page that use only `format_source*` and `Config` work with either.

## Format a string

```rust
let formatted = chloro::format_source("fn main(){let x=1;}\n");
assert_eq!(formatted, "fn main() {\n    let x = 1;\n}\n");
```

`format_source` formats with rustfmt's defaults at edition 2024, the same as `format_source_with_config(source, &Config::default())`.

The formatting functions return text, not errors. Source that does not parse, or that rustc's parser would reject, comes back unchanged, as rustfmt leaves such a file alone; so does a file with an inner `#![rustfmt::skip]` attribute, or any file when `disable_all_formatting` is set ([parse errors](<#parse-errors>) tells the first case from the others). To find out whether anything changed, compare the output with the input, or, to decide as rustfmt does, use `is_unchanged`:

```rust
let source = "fn main() {\n    let x = 1;\n}\n";
let needs_formatting = chloro::format_source(source) != source;
assert!(!needs_formatting);

// Not valid Rust: returned as written.
let broken = "fn main( {";
assert_eq!(chloro::format_source(broken), broken);

// `\r\n` line endings: the output has `\n` ones, and rustfmt counts the file as formatted.
let crlf = "fn main() {\r\n    let x = 1;\r\n}\r\n";
let config = chloro::Config::default();
let formatted = chloro::format_source_with_config(crlf, &config);
assert_eq!(formatted, source);
assert!(chloro::is_unchanged(crlf, &formatted, &config));
```

As in rustfmt, a byte order mark is dropped and `\r\n` in the input reads as `\n`; the output's line endings are set by `newline_style`, by default `\n` (the platform's for input with no line break). `is_unchanged` compares as rustfmt's `--check` does: under the default `newline_style = "Auto"`, a source that differs from its output only in `\r\n` line endings or a byte order mark is unchanged; under the other styles, the bytes must be equal.

## Parse errors

`try_format_source_with_config` returns the same text as `format_source_with_config`, or the syntax error for which that returns the source unchanged: the error rustfmt reports for a file it leaves alone, which the command line prints ([exit status](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/cli/#exit-status>)).

```rust
let config = chloro::Config::default();
let source = "fn main() {\n    let x = ;\n}\n";
let error = chloro::try_format_source_with_config(source, &config).unwrap_err();
assert_eq!((error.line(), error.column()), (2, 13));
assert_eq!(error.message(), "expected expression, found `;`");
assert_eq!(error.to_string(), "2:13: expected expression, found `;`");

// Left unchanged, but not an error.
let skipped = "#![rustfmt::skip]\nfn main(){}\n";
assert_eq!(chloro::try_format_source_with_config(skipped, &config).as_deref(), Ok(skipped));
```

The position is where rustc reports most syntax errors: the line, and the column in characters, both from 1, on the source with any byte order mark dropped and `\r\n` read as `\n`. `width()` is the number of characters the error covers on its line. The message is rust-analyzer's parser's, worded like rustc's where its tokens allow, or for syntax that rust-analyzer's parser accepts and rustc's rejects, "rustc's parser rejects this syntax". The error is found by parsing the source again once it has been refused, so the `try_` functions cost no more than the others on a source that parses. `chloro-core` has `try_format_source_with_config_parallel` and `try_format_source_with_unit_cache` for the entry points below.

## Options

```rust
let mut config = chloro::Config::default();
config.set("max_width", "80").unwrap();
config.set("edition", "2021").unwrap();
config.set("rustfmt_version", "1.8.0").unwrap();

let formatted = chloro::format_source_with_config("fn main(){}", &config);
assert_eq!(formatted, "fn main() {}\n");

// Unknown and unstable options are errors, with a message to show the user.
assert!(config.set("max_widht", "80").is_err());
assert!(config.set("wrap_comments", "true").is_err());
```

`Config::set` takes rustfmt's option names and value spellings; the fields of `Config` can also be set directly. [Configuration](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/configuration/index.md>) lists every option.

## One large file on several threads

```rust
use chloro_core::{Config, format_source_with_config, format_source_with_config_parallel};

let source = "use std::fmt;\nfn a(){}\nfn b(){}\nstruct S{x:u8}\n";
let config = Config::default();

let parallel = format_source_with_config_parallel(source, &config, 4);
assert_eq!(parallel, format_source_with_config(source, &config));
```

`format_source_with_config_parallel` formats the file's top-level items on up to `threads` scoped threads, started for the call and joined before it returns. The output is identical to `format_source_with_config`'s. With `threads <= 1`, or a file with fewer than two top-level items, no thread is started.

Starting threads costs more than it saves on a small file, and a program formatting many files usually does better to format several files at once with the sequential function. The command line splits only files of 128 KiB and more; see [Parallelism](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/parallelism/index.md>).

## A cache of formatted items

`format_source_with_unit_cache` is the parallel function with a cache of formatted top-level units, which you provide by implementing `UnitCache`. Each unit the cache does not hold is formatted and offered to `insert`; each one it does hold is reused. The output is identical to `format_source_with_config`'s.

```rust
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::collections::HashMap;

use chloro_core::{CachedUnit, Config, UnitCache, UnitKey, format_source_with_unit_cache};

/// Units in memory, keyed by everything a unit's output depends on.
#[derive(Default)]
struct MemoryUnits(RefCell<HashMap<(Vec<u8>, String), CachedUnit>>);

impl UnitCache for MemoryUnits {
    fn get(&self, key: &UnitKey<'_>) -> Option<CachedUnit> {
        let key = (key.context().to_vec(), key.text().to_owned());
        self.0.borrow().get(&key).cloned()
    }

    fn insert(&self, key: &UnitKey<'_>, unit: CachedUnit) {
        let key = (key.context().to_vec(), key.text().to_owned());
        self.0.borrow_mut().insert(key, unit);
    }
}

let units = MemoryUnits::default();
let config = Config::default();

let before = "fn a(){}\nfn b(){}\n";
let after = "fn a(){}\nfn b(){1}\n"; // only `b` changed

assert_eq!(format_source_with_unit_cache(before, &config, 1, &units), "fn a() {}\nfn b() {}\n");
// The second call formats `b` and reuses `a`.
assert_eq!(format_source_with_unit_cache(after, &config, 1, &units), "fn a() {}\nfn b() {\n    1\n}\n");
```

The rules for an implementation:

- `get` may return a unit only if `insert` was given it for a key with equal `context()` and `text()`. Keying by both, or by a collision-resistant hash of both, satisfies this.
- The key does not identify the build of `chloro-core`. A cache kept across processes must also be keyed by the build (the command line names its cache file by the digest of its executable). `CachedUnit::to_bytes` and `CachedUnit::from_bytes` serialise a unit for such a store.
- The formatter calls the cache from the calling thread only, so the implementation needs no synchronisation of its own.

## Parse without formatting

```rust
use chloro_core::{Config, parse_only};

let elements = parse_only("fn main() {}", &Config::default());
assert!(elements.is_some());
assert_eq!(parse_only("fn main( {", &Config::default()), None);
```

`parse_only` runs the steps formatting starts with (normalisation, lexing, parsing, building the syntax tree, and the checks for syntax rustc's parser handles differently) and returns the number of nodes and tokens in the file's tree, or `None` where formatting would return the source unchanged without formatting it. It exists to measure the parser's share of the formatter's cost, and to check quickly whether chloro would format a file at all.

## Debug output

`chloro_core::chloro_debug!` prints to standard error when debug output is enabled, either with the `CHLORO_DEBUG` environment variable at start-up or with `chloro_core::debug::set_debug(true)`. It is for developing chloro itself.

## The syntax tree

`chloro_core::cst` is the flat syntax tree the formatter reads, with a typed layer that keeps rust-analyzer's `ast` names. It is public so that the tools in `chloro-core/examples` can use it, and is not re-exported by `chloro`. [Parsing and the syntax tree](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/architecture/parsing/index.md>) describes it.

# Reference

# <kbd>chloro</kbd>

Reference for the `chloro` command. The [Command line guide](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/cli/index.md>) explains how the options work together.

## Usage

```text
Usage: chloro [OPTIONS] [SOURCES]...

A Rust code formatter reproducing `rustfmt --edition 2024`.

Arguments:
  [SOURCES]...       Files or directories to format (default: '.', the current
                     directory). Directories are walked for .rs files, skipping
                     hidden entries and cache directories such as target/

Options:
  -c, --check        Check if files need formatting (exit 1 if so)
  -w, --write        Write formatted output back to files
  -v, --verbose      Show verbose output
      --config OPTS  rustfmt options as comma-separated key=value pairs
      --no-cache     Format every file; do not read or write the caches
      --unit-cache   Also cache each formatted top-level item, so that a changed
                     file formats only the items not seen before (off by default)
      --cache-dir D  Cache directory (default: $CHLORO_CACHE_DIR, else the
                     user cache directory, e.g. ~/.cache/chloro)
      --threads N    Threads to use (default: one per core)
  -V, --version      Print the version and exit
  -h, --help         Show this help message

Examples:
  # Format a single file and print to stdout
  chloro src/lib.rs

  # Format multiple files
  chloro src/*.rs

  # Check if files need formatting
  chloro --check src/

  # Format files in-place
  chloro --write src/

  # Format with rustfmt options
  chloro --config max_width=80,tab_spaces=2 src/lib.rs

Cache:
  chloro records the content hash of every file it finds already formatted,
  keyed by the chloro binary and the --config options, and skips formatting
  files whose content it has seen formatted before. The output and exit code
  are the same with and without the cache.

  With --unit-cache, chloro also keeps the formatted output of each top-level
  item (or group of `use`/`mod`/`extern crate` items) under the same key and
  the item's text, and formats only the items of a changed file it has not
  seen. The output and exit code are the same. It is off by default: a run that
  finds nothing in it (a cold CI run) costs 10-15% more with it on.
```

Which files a directory contributes is described in the guide, under [Sources](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/cli/#sources>).

## Options

### <kbd>--check</kbd> / <kbd>-c</kbd>

Format every file without writing anything. Exit with status 1, and print `Error: N file(s) need formatting`, if any file's formatted text differs from its contents.

### <kbd>--write</kbd> / <kbd>-w</kbd>

Write each file whose formatted text differs from its contents. Without `--check` or `--write`, every formatted file is printed to standard output.

### <kbd>--config OPTS</kbd>

rustfmt options as comma-separated `key=value` pairs, with rustfmt's names and value spellings, plus `rustfmt_version`. An invalid option is an error before any file is read. [Configuration](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/configuration/index.md>) lists them.

### <kbd>--threads N</kbd>

The number of worker threads. The default, or `0`, is one per core. Files of 128 KiB and more also have their top-level items formatted on this many threads. [Parallelism](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/parallelism/index.md>).

### <kbd>--no-cache</kbd>

Neither read nor write the fixed-point cache or the unit cache. [Caching](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/caching/index.md>).

### <kbd>--unit-cache</kbd>

Also cache the formatted text of each top-level item, so that a changed file formats only the items not seen before. Off by default; overridden by `--no-cache`. [Caching](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/caching/#the-unit-cache>).

### <kbd>--cache-dir DIR</kbd>

The directory of the caches. Default: `$CHLORO_CACHE_DIR`, else `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/chloro`, else the platform's user cache directory (`~/.cache/chloro`, `~/Library/Caches/chloro`, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\chloro\cache`).

### <kbd>--verbose</kbd> / <kbd>-v</kbd>

Report, on standard error, the sources and mode, the cache file and its size, the number of files and threads, each file as it is processed, and a summary at the end.

### <kbd>--version</kbd> / <kbd>-V</kbd>

Print the version and exit. The plain version, `chloro 0.9.0`, is printed only by a build of the release itself; any other build is marked as a development build, with what is known of its source:

| output | built from |
| --- | --- |
| `chloro 0.9.0` | the release: the commit tagged `chloro-v0.9.0` with no uncommitted changes, or the crate published to crates.io |
| `chloro 0.9.0-dev (2f9b060)` | another commit (`2f9b060`) of a git checkout |
| `chloro 0.9.0-dev (2f9b060, dirty)` | a checkout with uncommitted changes to the files that go into the binary |
| `chloro 0.9.0-dev (unknown source)` | a copy of the source with no git repository or packaging record, which cannot be checked |

The version is the crate's version; `-dev` is added only to this output. The check is made when chloro is compiled (`chloro/build.rs`), from the local repository: the build reruns when HEAD moves, a tag changes, or a source file changes, and `--version` reads nothing at run time.

A binary installed with `just reinstall` also prints its build ID, a hash of the source it was built from, as in `chloro 0.9.0-dev (2f9b060, dirty, build <id>)` ([Benchmarking](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/maintainers/benchmarking/#on-any-cargo-project-just-vs-rustfmt>)).

### <kbd>--help</kbd> / <kbd>-h</kbd>

Print the help text and exit.

## Exit status

| status | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | success; with `--check`, nothing needs formatting |
| 1 | `--check` found files to format, or a file does not parse ([errors](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/cli/#exit-status>)), or a file could not be read or written, or a source does not exist, or `--config` or the arguments were invalid |

## Environment

| variable | effect |
| --- | --- |
| `CHLORO_CACHE_DIR` | the cache directory, when `--cache-dir` is not given |
| `XDG_CACHE_HOME` | the parent of the default cache directory, when set |
| `CHLORO_TRACE` | a file to write a per-worker timeline of the run to |

# Rust API

The Rust API is documented on docs.rs. This page lists the public entry points and where each is explained on this site.

[**docs.rs/chloro**The library facade and the command-line crate.](<https://docs.rs/chloro>) [**docs.rs/chloro-core**The formatter, its entry points, the configuration and the syntax tree.](<https://docs.rs/chloro-core>)

## Formatting

| item | in `chloro` | in `chloro-core` |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `format_source(source: &str) -> String` | yes | yes | rustfmt's defaults, edition 2024 |
| `format_source_with_config(source: &str, config: &Config) -> String` | yes | yes | any options |
| `format_source_with_config_parallel(source, config, threads) -> String` |  | yes | top-level items on up to `threads` threads; [guide](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/library/#one-large-file-on-several-threads>) |
| `format_source_with_unit_cache(source, config, threads, cache: &dyn UnitCache) -> String` |  | yes | reuses formatted items; [guide](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/library/#a-cache-of-formatted-items>) |
| `try_format_source_with_config(source, config) -> Result<String, ParseError>` | yes | yes | the same text, or the syntax error; [guide](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/library/#parse-errors>) |
| `try_format_source_with_config_parallel(source, config, threads)`, `try_format_source_with_unit_cache(source, config, threads, cache)` |  | yes | the same for the parallel and cached functions |
| `is_unchanged(source, formatted, config) -> bool` | yes | yes | whether rustfmt counts `formatted` as a change to `source` (line endings, byte order mark); [guide](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/library/#format-a-string>) |
| `ParseError` | yes | yes | `message()`, `line()`, `column()` (from 1, in characters), `width()`; `Display` as `line:column: message` |
| `parse_only(source, config) -> Option<usize>` |  | yes | the parse alone; [guide](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/library/#parse-without-formatting>) |

Every formatting function returns the source unchanged when it does not parse, when rustc's parser would reject it, when it has an inner `#![rustfmt::skip]`, or when `disable_all_formatting` is set; the `try_` functions return the error instead in the first two cases. All of them return the same text for the same source and configuration.

## Configuration

| item |  |
| --- | --- |
| `Config` | one public field per stable rustfmt option, plus `rustfmt_version`; `Default` is rustfmt's defaults |
| `Config::set(&mut self, key: &str, value: &str) -> Result<(), String>` | set an option by rustfmt's name and spelling |
| `chloro_core::formatter::config::{NewlineStyle, Heuristics, Edition, StyleEdition, MatchArmLeadingPipe, Density, RustfmtVersion}` | the enum-valued options |

[Configuration](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/configuration/index.md>) lists every option and its default.

## The unit cache

| item |  |
| --- | --- |
| `trait UnitCache { fn get(&self, key: &UnitKey<'_>) -> Option<CachedUnit>; fn insert(&self, key: &UnitKey<'_>, unit: CachedUnit); }` | the store `format_source_with_unit_cache` reads and fills |
| `UnitKey` | what a unit's output depends on: `context()` (configuration, skip names, crate version) and `text()` |
| `CachedUnit` | one formatted unit; `to_bytes` and `from_bytes` serialise it |

## Lower level

| item |  |
| --- | --- |
| `chloro_core::cst` | the flat syntax tree and its typed layer ([Parsing](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/architecture/parsing/index.md>)) |
| `chloro_core::chloro_debug!`, `chloro_core::debug` | debug output to standard error, for developing chloro |
| `chloro_core::formatter::printer` | a printer trait from chloro's earlier formatter, unused by the current one |

# rustfmt compatibility

chloro aims to produce exactly the bytes rustfmt produces. This page lists what its output has been compared against, how the comparisons were made, and what they do not cover.

Each result below compares chloro's output with the output of a named rustfmt binary on the same source with the same options. The comparisons cover the corpora and options listed here; they do not show that chloro and rustfmt agree on every possible input.

## Reference versions

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| rustfmt release reproduced by default | `rustfmt 1.9.0-stable (2d8144b788 2026-07-07)`, shipped with Rust 1.97.0 |
| second release, with `rustfmt_version = "1.8.0"` | `rustfmt 1.8.0-stable (6b00bc3880 2025-06-23)`, shipped with Rust 1.88.0 |
| how rustfmt is run | `rustfmt --edition 2024` (or the edition under test) on standard input, with no `rustfmt.toml` |
| what counts as identical | the same bytes; where rustfmt rejects a file, the expected output is the input, unchanged |

## Results

| what varies | values | corpus | identical |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| rustfmt release | 1.9.0, the default | 1220 rust-analyzer source files, default options | 1220 of 1220, none non-idempotent |
| rustfmt release | 1.8.0 | the same | 1220 of 1220, none non-idempotent |
| stable options | 31 non-default values of 24 options (below) | the same, every file rustfmt accepts under the option | every file (1022 of 1022 for each value at edition 2024) |
| edition | 2015, 2018, 2021, 2024 | the same | 838/838, 843/843, 844/844, 1022/1022 |
| style edition | 2015, 2021, 2024 | the same | 1022/1022 each |
| code chloro was not developed on | default options, rustfmt 1.9.0 | 20,850 files of 577 crates from crates.io | 20,540 of the 20,540 files rustfmt formats |
| the same at rustfmt 1.8.0 | default options | 20,019 files of 559 crates, measured before the last conformance fixes | 20,007 of 20,019: 9 files the later fixes target, 3 that both releases reject |

Notes on the table:

- **The rust-analyzer corpus.** 1238 `.rs` files from rust-analyzer are checked in under `chloro-core/tests/conformance/fixtures/`, with rustfmt's output for each stored as a snapshot. 1220 of them are compared; 216 of those are files rustfmt rejects, where the expected output is the input.
- **Non-idempotent** counts files whose chloro output, formatted again, changes. None does.
- **The option rows** count only the files rustfmt accepts under the option, so an edition that rejects more files has a smaller denominator.
- **The registry corpus** is 577 crates downloaded from crates.io by a committed manifest, compared live against rustfmt. Every change merged during the performance work was also checked to leave the output of every file in both corpora unchanged, except for the files a conformance fix was meant to change.

### Options

The option values compared with rustfmt 1.9.0:

`max_width` 80 and 120, `hard_tabs`, `tab_spaces` 2, `use_small_heuristics` Max and Off, `fn_call_width` 40, `chain_width` 40, `struct_lit_width` 0, `array_width` 30, `single_line_if_else_max_width` 0, `single_line_let_else_max_width` 0, `reorder_imports` false, `reorder_modules` false, `remove_nested_parens` false, `short_array_element_width_threshold` 4, `match_arm_leading_pipes` Always and Preserve, `fn_params_layout` Vertical and Compressed, `match_block_trailing_comma`, `merge_derives` false, `use_try_shorthand`, `use_field_init_shorthand`, `force_explicit_abi` false, `newline_style` Windows, `style_edition` 2021 and 2015, `edition` 2021, 2018 and 2015.

`attr_fn_like_width`, `struct_variant_width` and `disable_all_formatting` are accepted but not part of the comparison.

## rustfmt releases

rustfmt 1.8.0 and 1.9.0 differ in two ways, and `rustfmt_version` reproduces both:

- **Formatting.** A handful of constructs come out differently, for example raw labels in `break 'r#a` (1.8.0 drops the `r#`), a labelled block as a closure body, `use self::self;`, `super let`, the import order of `_`-prefixed names at editions before 2024, and a `macro_rules!` body that is a single `const { .. }` block.
- **Acceptance.** Each release's rustfmt formats only what its own toolchain's parser accepts. For example, rustfmt 1.8.0 formats `if a && let …` at edition 2021 and `impl !Trait {}`, which 1.9.0 rejects and leaves alone, and rejects `[const]` bounds, which 1.9.0 formats.

On the rust-analyzer corpus at edition 2024, the two releases give identical output on all but one of the files both accept. A reproducer for each difference, at both releases and editions 2021 and 2024, is in `chloro-core/tests/conformance/rustfmt-versions/`; the [rustfmt versions record](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-14-autoresearch/rustfmt-versions.md>) names each class and the rustfmt change behind it.

rustfmt 1.7.0 and earlier are refused: 1.7.0 has no 2024 Style Guide rules, and 540 of the 981 rust-analyzer files both releases accept come out differently. Nightly rustfmt is not compared.

## What is not covered

- **`rustfmt.toml`.** chloro reads no configuration file. Options come from `--config` or `Config`.
- **Unstable options.** chloro always uses rustfmt's defaults for them, and setting one to another value is an error ([Configuration](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/configuration/#unstable-rustfmt-options>)).
- **rustfmt's command line.** There are no `--emit`, `--files-with-diff`, `--edition` or standard input modes; `--check` reports a count, not a diff. Editions are set with `--config edition=…`.
- **Out-of-line modules.** rustfmt formats the files a crate's `mod` declarations lead to; chloro formats the files and directories you name, whatever modules they declare.
- **Syntax rust-analyzer's parser cannot represent.** chloro parses with rust-analyzer's parser and rebuilds the tree for the cases where rustc's parser accepts something rust-analyzer rejects. Two such constructs remain (below).
- **Error reporting.** Both tools leave a file that does not parse unchanged, print its error and exit with status 1. chloro's message is rust-analyzer's parser's, worded like rustc's where its tokens allow, at the position rustc reports for most errors; it prints the first error of a file only, without rustc's notes and suggestions ([command line](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/cli/#exit-status>)). Where rustfmt fails with an internal error but still writes output, chloro writes the same output and reports no error.

## Known differences

Six cases are recorded and open in the [conformance ledger](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-14-autoresearch/conformance-ledger.md>):

|  | what | effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 19 | A doc comment before an expression in an argument list, array, `let` or statement position: rustc treats it as an attribute of the expression and rustfmt formats it with the expression; chloro leaves it where it is. | Layout differs around the comment. No registry file is affected; rustc warns about such comments (`unused_doc_comments`). |
| 20 | Edition-2015 trait methods with anonymous parameters, `fn f(usize);`, which rust-analyzer's parser rejects. | chloro reports a parse error and leaves the file unchanged; rustfmt formats it. |
| 21 | rustfmt's internal error on one file of rustyline 14.0.0. | rustfmt exits with an error and writes the output chloro writes. |
| 22 | rustfmt's run time on a 47 KB generated file of pest\_meta 2.9.2. | rustfmt takes over nine minutes and chloro 0.2 s, for identical output. |
| 23 | Files where rustfmt's own output is not a fixed point (eight known). | chloro's output matches rustfmt's at every pass. |
| 24 | Minor forms: a trailing comma in `builtin # offset_of(…)`, which rust-analyzer rejects. | chloro reports a parse error and leaves the file unchanged. |

A difference not listed here is a bug: please [open an issue](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/issues>) with the input, the options, and the rustfmt version.

## Reproducing the comparison

The `rustfmt` on `PATH` is the 1.9.0 reference; `rustup run 1.88.0 rustfmt` is the 1.8.0 one.

```sh
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example conform -- -i              # 1220 files against the 1.9.0 snapshots
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example conform -- -i -V 1.8.0     # the same at rustfmt_version = 1.8.0
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example config_matrix -- -n 1220   # 31 option values against live rustfmt
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example config_matrix -- --root ~/.cargo/registry/src -n 30000 default
cargo test -p chloro-core --test conformance batch                      # regenerate the snapshots
```

[Development](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/maintainers/development/#conformance>) explains the snapshots and how they are regenerated.

# Performance

chloro's speed and memory use measured against rustfmt, the conditions of the measurements, and what was not measured.

## Summary

Against rustfmt 1.9.0, checking already-formatted crates:

- **One core:** 0.21–0.35 of rustfmt's wall time on each of nine crates, with every chloro run faster than every rustfmt run.
- **Four cores:** 0.08–0.17 of rustfmt's wall time, chloro using one thread per core and rustfmt running as it does (one thread).
- **Memory:** 4–10 MiB peak resident memory on one core and 5–23 MiB on four, against rustfmt's 43–86 MiB.
- **Unchanged trees:** a warm `--check` of 1238 formatted files in 16.2 ms on four cores.

Against chloro 0.8.0, the release before the performance work, the formatter executes 66% fewer instructions on the same files and formats 2.7 times as many bytes per second on one core.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Conditions**
>
> All figures are from measurement [M6](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-14-autoresearch/measurements/m6-quiet-host.md>) (2026-10-17), taken with `benchmarks/compare_rustfmt.sh` on an idle 4-core KVM guest (Intel Xeon, 2.80 GHz class, Linux), with rustfmt `1.9.0-stable (2d8144b788 2026-07-07)` and chloro built with the workspace's release profile. Each cell is 30 timed runs with hyperfine (15 runs in each of two rounds, the command order reversed in the second), after 2 warm-up runs. Both tools check copies of the same files, formatted by rustfmt first, with `--check`; chloro's cache is off. One-core rows pin both tools to the same core. Ratios are of mean wall times.
>
> Absolute times depend on this host and varied by up to 20–40% between measurement sessions, so compare the ratios, which were taken with both tools interleaved in the same session.

## Per crate

| crate | files | size | ratio, one core | ratio, four cores | rustfmt, one core | chloro, one core |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `hir` | 15 | 646 KB | 0.262 | 0.086 | 327.9 | 85.9 |
| `hir-ty` | 122 | 2876 KB | 0.252 | 0.077 | 1021.9 | 257.9 |
| `ide-db` | 33 | 1169 KB | 0.214 | 0.084 | 369.8 | 79.1 |
| `syntax` | 33 | 405 KB | 0.324 | 0.112 | 145.7 | 47.2 |
| `parser` | 28 | 235 KB | 0.323 | 0.117 | 82.5 | 26.6 |
| tokio 1.53.3 | 49 | 215 KB | 0.318 | 0.165 | 54.4 | 17.3 |
| regex-syntax 0.8.11 | 33 | 1647 KB | 0.324 | 0.111 | 543.3 | 175.9 |
| clap\_builder 4.6.7 | 57 | 944 KB | 0.318 | 0.126 | 210.2 | 66.9 |
| winnow 0.7.15 | 61 | 1005 KB | 0.345 | 0.127 | 211.5 | 73.0 |

The ratios are chloro's mean wall time divided by rustfmt's; the last two columns are mean wall times in milliseconds. The first five crates are from rust-analyzer, whose files make up chloro's conformance corpus. The other four come from crates.io and were not used during chloro's development.

## A large workspace: ruff

A single measurement of the whole [ruff](<https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff>) workspace, taken with `just vs-ruff` ([Benchmarking](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/maintainers/benchmarking/#on-any-cargo-project-just-vs-rustfmt>)) on a 20-core workstation, against `cargo fmt` with the rustfmt ruff's toolchain pins, `1.10.0-stable (b940084d7e 2026-09-28)`. Both tools check the 2,008 files `cargo fmt --all` formats, in an already-formatted checkout, with hyperfine: 5 timed runs each after 1 warm-up, not pinned to cores, chloro with its cache off.

| command | wall time, mean ± σ | share of `cargo fmt`'s | peak memory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `chloro --check`, 20 threads (the default) | 212.3 ± 4.8 ms | 0.038 | 89.9 MiB |
| `chloro --check --threads 1` | 1598.3 ± 12.6 ms | 0.284 | 16.2 MiB |
| `cargo fmt --all -- --check` | 5633.0 ± 104.8 ms | 1 | 194.5 MiB |

- The one-thread row is the like-for-like comparison, since rustfmt formats on one thread: 0.28 of `cargo fmt`'s time, inside the one-core range of the nine crates above, though on a different machine and with fewer runs.
- Peak memory is that of the largest single process, which for `cargo fmt` is rustfmt.
- The recipe passes the file list to chloro through `xargs`, which can split a list this long into several chloro runs, one after another; their start-up and lost parallelism count against chloro ([\#99](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/issues/99>)).
- The outputs agree on all but one file. In a separate check of ruff at commit `8d122c1` (2,023 files) with the same rustfmt, `cargo fmt --check` found nothing to change and `chloro --check` reported one file, which has three `\r\n` line endings among `\n` ones: rustfmt counts it as formatted and leaves it as it is, and chloro 0.9.0 rewrote it. chloro now decides as rustfmt does ([\#97](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/issues/97>)).

## Other measurements

| quantity | chloro | rustfmt 1.9.0 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| in-process throughput, one core, 1238 files (13.9 MB), best of 5 | 12.0–13.2 MB/s; 14.5–15.1 profile-guided; chloro 0.8.0 4.4–4.9 in the same window | not measured in process |
| 287 small files in one invocation (rust-analyzer's `parser/test_data`) | 0.23 of rustfmt's wall time on one core, 0.12 on four |  |
| one 13-byte file (process start-up) | 1.8 ms, one core | 11.7 ms |
| `--check` of an unchanged 1238-file tree, warm cache | 16.2 ms on four cores, 32.1 ms on one | no cache |
| the same with `--no-cache` | 356 ms on four cores, 1290 ms on one |  |
| one file of 128 KiB or more, four threads against one | 1.1–1.7 times as fast on the five largest corpus files, for 1.09–1.32 times the CPU | single-threaded |
| a 2,000-byte file of closures nested 16 deep | 5.5 M instructions; chloro 0.8.0: 242.5 M |  |

## Instruction counts

Wall-time measurements on a shared virtual machine are noisy, so chloro's performance work was guided by the number of instructions executed, which barely varies between runs. The counts come from callgrind (`benchmarks/profile.sh`) on two fixed samples of 49 files each, one from the conformance corpus and one from four crates.io crates:

| sample | chloro 0.8.0 | now | profile-guided build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 49 rust-analyzer files (650 KB) | 587,988,576 | 202,822,485 (−65.5%) | 170,069,599 (−71.1%) |
| 49 crates.io files (732 KB) | 688,589,271 | 255,681,198 (−62.9%) | 219,987,557 (−68.1%) |

Of what remains, lexing and parsing are 34% of the instructions on the first sample and 42% on the second.

## Profile-guided builds

`benchmarks/pgo.sh` builds chloro with profile-guided optimisation, training on the conformance corpus. On these measurements the profile-guided build ran in 0.18–0.33 of rustfmt's wall time on one core and 0.07–0.16 on four. The release workflow applies the same training to the targets whose runners execute them natively; see [Releasing](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/maintainers/releasing/#profile-guided-builds>).

## What was not measured

- macOS and Windows: the measurements other than ruff's are from x86-64 Linux.
- rustfmt's throughput in process: rustfmt is only timed as a process, including its start-up (loading `librustc_driver` costs it about 30 ms and 34 MiB).
- Memory bandwidth. Apart from the ruff measurement, nothing was measured on more than four cores.
- Unformatted input. The inputs are formatted by rustfmt first, because rustfmt's `--check` builds a diff of every file that would change, and that would add the cost of the diff to rustfmt's time.

## Optimisations

chloro makes the same formatting decisions as rustfmt, so it does the same work, with less overhead. It reads syntax from one flat array instead of pointer-linked nodes, lexes and builds the tree in one pass, memoises rewrites that deep nesting would otherwise repeat, proves from a node's tokens when a one-line layout cannot fit instead of rendering it to find out, keeps short-lived strings in a per-thread arena, formats files and large files' items on all cores, and skips files it has already seen formatted. [How it works](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/architecture/overview/index.md>) explains each of these.

## Reproducing

Needs `hyperfine` 2.0, `taskset`, `jq` and `python3`; `valgrind` and `setarch` for instruction counts; and rustfmt 1.9.0 on `PATH`.

```sh
cargo build --release -p chloro --features cli && cargo build --release -p chloro-core --examples
benchmarks/compare_rustfmt.sh -r 15 -w 2 --rounds 2 --core 3   # wall, CPU, RSS per workload; tables in report.md
benchmarks/profile.sh --core 3                                 # instruction count on the 49-file sample
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example bench -- -n 5     # in-process MB/s on the corpus
```

[Benchmarking](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/maintainers/benchmarking/index.md>) describes the workloads and the scripts. The six measurement records, M1 to M6, and the experiments behind each change are in the [project history](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/history/index.md>).

# Changelog

All notable changes to chloro, for people who use it. The format follows [Keep a Changelog](<https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/>), and versions follow [Semantic Versioning](<https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html>). `chloro` and `chloro-core` are released together at the same version.

This file is written by hand, and each release's GitHub notes are taken from it. Until 0.7.5 each crate also had a commit-level changelog generated by release-plz: [chloro/CHANGELOG.md](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/chloro/CHANGELOG.md>) and [chloro-core/CHANGELOG.md](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/chloro-core/CHANGELOG.md>).

## [Unreleased](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/compare/chloro-v0.9.0...HEAD>)

### Added

- `try_format_source_with_config`, `try_format_source_with_config_parallel` and `try_format_source_with_unit_cache` return the formatted text, or the `ParseError` for which the other functions return the source unchanged: its message, line and column. `chloro` re-exports `try_format_source_with_config` and `ParseError`.
- `is_unchanged(source, formatted, config)` tells whether rustfmt counts a formatting function's output as a change to the source (see *Fixed*); `chloro` re-exports it.

### Changed

- A directory walk skips hidden entries (`.git/`, `.hidden.rs`) and cache directories, those with a `CACHEDIR.TAG` file such as Cargo's `target/`, so `chloro --check` at the root of a project no longer formats its build output ([\#90](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/issues/90>)). A path named on the command line is always used.

### Fixed

- A file that does not parse, or that contains syntax rustc's parser rejects, is reported as rustfmt reports it: its first error is printed in rustc's layout, nothing is printed or written for the file, and the exit status is 1, in every mode ([\#87](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/issues/87>)). It was left unchanged as before, but silently and with exit status 0, and recorded in the cache as formatted.
- Under the default `newline_style = "Auto"`, a file that differs from its formatted output only in its `\r\n` line endings (all of them, or a stray few among `\n` ones) or a byte order mark is formatted, as rustfmt decides: `--check` passes and `--write` leaves it as it is ([\#97](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/issues/97>)). chloro reported such a file and rewrote it with `\n` line endings.
- `--help` gives the default source as the current directory, which it is, not `src` ([\#91](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/issues/91>)).

## [0.9.0](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/compare/chloro-v0.8.0...chloro-v0.9.0>) - 2026-10-17

The performance and conformance work of [\#88](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/pull/88>). Every output is identical to 0.8.0's except for the conformance fixes listed under *Fixed*. The measurements behind the figures below are described on the [Performance](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/performance/>) page.

### Added

- The command line formats files on every core, one worker per core, taking the largest files first; `--threads N` sets the number of workers.
- Files of 128 KiB or more also have their top-level items formatted on several threads, with identical output.
- A cache of file contents known to be formatted: a later `--check` or `--write` skips them without parsing. It is keyed by the chloro binary and the configuration, lives in the user cache directory, and does not change any output or exit status. `--no-cache` turns it off; `--cache-dir` and `CHLORO_CACHE_DIR` move it.
- `--unit-cache`, an opt-in cache of formatted top-level items, so that a changed file formats only the items not seen before.
- The `rustfmt_version` option reproduces rustfmt 1.8.0 (as shipped with Rust 1.88) as well as 1.9.0, the default: `--config rustfmt_version=1.8.0`.
- `#[rustfmt::skip::macros(..)]` and `#[rustfmt::skip::attributes(..)]` are honoured.
- `CHLORO_TRACE=FILE` writes a per-worker timeline of a command-line run.
- `-V`/`--version` prints the version. A build from anything but the release's tagged commit is marked as a development build, with its commit and whether it had uncommitted changes: `chloro 0.8.0-dev (2f9b060, dirty)`.
- `chloro-core` library functions: `format_source_with_config_parallel` (one file's items on several threads), `format_source_with_unit_cache` with the `UnitCache` trait, `UnitKey` and `CachedUnit` (reuse formatted items across calls), and `parse_only`. The existing functions are unchanged.
- Release binaries for the targets GitHub's runners build natively are built with profile-guided optimisation.
- A documentation website at [https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/>), and this changelog.

### Changed

- Formatting is faster. Against rustfmt 1.9.0 on nine crates, chloro takes 0.21–0.35 of rustfmt's wall time on one core and 0.08–0.17 on four. Against 0.8.0, the formatter executes 66% fewer instructions on the same files and formats 2.7 times as many bytes per second on one core.
- On the whole ruff workspace (2,008 files), chloro took 0.28 of `cargo fmt`'s wall time on one thread and 0.038 on 20.
- Peak memory on the same crates is 4–10 MiB on one core, against 6–29 MiB for 0.8.0 (rustfmt: 43–86 MiB).
- Nested closures no longer slow formatting down superlinearly: a 2 KB file of closures nested 16 deep takes 5.5 million instructions, against 242.5 million in 0.8.0.
- `chloro-core`'s runtime dependency tree is 18 crates, from 37. rust-analyzer's syntax tree crates (`ra_ap_syntax`, `rowan`) are no longer runtime dependencies; the formatter reads its own flat syntax tree. `bumpalo` is added; `ra-ap-rustc_lexer` and `rustc-literal-escaper`, already in the tree through `ra_ap_parser`, are now named directly.
- The release profile uses fat link-time optimisation and one codegen unit.
- A file reachable twice on the command line (named twice, or through a symlink) is formatted once.

### Fixed

Output now matches rustfmt 1.9.0 on all 1220 rust-analyzer conformance files (1219 in 0.8.0) and on all 20,540 files of a 577-crate registry corpus that rustfmt formats (20,526 of 20,536 before):

- Nested blocks in a macro definition get rustfmt's trailing semicolons.
- A repeat array, `[x; n]`, is not laid out as a block.
- Doc comments inside macro arguments are formatted as rustfmt formats them.
- Files containing syntax rustc's parser rejects are left unchanged, as rustfmt leaves them: `<-`, `..a = b`, `a..=` without an end, an ambiguous `+` in a type, an unbraced const parameter default, `builtin #` syntax, pattern parameters in an edition-2015 trait method, a misplaced doc comment, and a C string literal before edition 2021.
- Files with syntax rustc accepts but rust-analyzer's parser rejects are now formatted: a parenthesised first bound of a bare trait object (`Box<(Copy) + Send>`), a float literal as a field name, a `const` block item, `impl impl Trait {}`, and an unknown literal prefix before edition 2021.
- A panic while formatting on a worker thread is reported with its own message.

## [0.8.0](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/compare/chloro-v0.7.5...chloro-v0.8.0>) - 2026-10-11

A rewrite of the formatter: a module-for-module port of rustfmt 1.9.0 onto rust-analyzer's syntax trees ([\#85](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/pull/85>)). Output matches rustfmt on 1219 of the 1220 rust-analyzer conformance files, against 233 before.

### Added

- `Config`, with a public field for every stable rustfmt option and `Config::set` taking rustfmt's option names and values; `format_source_with_config` and `Config` are re-exported from `chloro`.
- `--config key=value,...` on the command line, validated before any file is read.
- `#[rustfmt::skip]` on files and nodes.
- `extern crate` items ([\#80](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/pull/80>)) and `if let` chains ([\#82](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/pull/82>)).

### Changed

- The formatting rules are rustfmt's: files rustfmt rejects are returned unchanged, unstable rustfmt options keep their defaults, and `style_edition` follows `edition` unless set.
