- Method chains are no longer "snuggled" ([\#83](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/pull/83>)).

### Fixed

- Comments on `use` items are kept ([\#81](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/pull/81>)).

## [0.7.5](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/compare/chloro-v0.7.4...chloro-v0.7.5>) - 2025-12-05

### Fixed

- Long comments are no longer split at the maximum line width ([\#78](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/pull/78>)).

## [0.7.0](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/releases/tag/chloro-v0.7.0>) – [0.7.4](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/compare/chloro-v0.6.8...chloro-v0.7.4>) - 2025-11-26 to 2025-12-05

Incremental work on the hand-written formatter that preceded the rustfmt port: comments kept in enums, structs, macro calls and before items; `use` and `mod` ordering as in the 2024 style; struct literals, enum variants, `extern` blocks, `impl` blocks and more expressions. The per-crate changelogs list each release.

Nested imports, generics and `where` clauses, struct literals and function formatting, and comment whitespace handling; a conformance report against rust-analyzer's sources in the README.

The first releases: a proof-of-concept formatter over rust-analyzer's `rowan` trees, with library and command-line interfaces.

# How it works

# How it works

chloro is rustfmt's formatting code ported onto a parser that is available as an ordinary library, then optimised. This page gives an overview of how a file goes from source text to formatted output.

## Background

rustfmt is built on the Rust compiler: it parses a file with rustc's parser into rustc's abstract syntax tree, then rewrites each node, trying candidate layouts in a fixed order and keeping the first that fits the width. Its output is the product of a few hundred interacting width heuristics and fallbacks. chloro's first versions tried to reproduce that output rule by rule from observation, and matched rustfmt on 233 of the 1220 conformance files. Reproducing a few hundred interacting heuristics one rule at a time from their output did not come close to rustfmt.

So chloro ports rustfmt instead. The formatter in `chloro-core` follows rustfmt 1.9.0's source module by module, keeping its control flow, names and comments, so that every formatting decision can be checked against the rustfmt code it reproduces. The difference is the parser: the syntax comes from rust-analyzer's parser (`ra_ap_parser`), which is published as a library, rather than from rustc, which is not. A thin adaptation layer presents rust-analyzer's syntax in the shape rustfmt's code expects.

The port matched rustfmt on 1219 of the 1220 files, and later on all 1220. The performance work that followed left every output byte unchanged and made the formatter 2.7 times as fast.

## The pipeline

From source text to formatted text. Each box names the module that does the step.

1. **Normalise.** A leading byte order mark is dropped and `\r\n` reads as `\n`, as rustc's source map does.
2. **Lex and parse.** chloro's own lexer front end turns the text into rust-analyzer's tokens in one pass over `rustc_lexer`, and rust-analyzer's parser turns them into a stream of events. A text with a lexer error goes through rust-analyzer's own lexer instead, so errors are reported the same way.
3. **Build the tree.** The parser's events become one flat array of nodes and tokens over the source text, with comments and whitespace attached where rust-analyzer attaches them. [Parsing and the syntax tree](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/architecture/parsing/index.md>) describes the tree.
4. **Match rustc's parser.** rustfmt formats exactly the files rustc's parser accepts, and the two parsers do not accept exactly the same syntax. Where rust-analyzer rejects syntax rustc accepts, the tree is rebuilt with the node rustc would build (`rustc_syntax`); where rust-analyzer accepts syntax rustc rejects, the file is returned unchanged (`rustc_compat`). A file that neither parser accepts is returned unchanged, as rustfmt returns it.
5. **Visit and rewrite.** The visitor walks items and statements in source order, copying the comments and blank lines between them from the source, and the ported rewrite modules format each node. [The formatting engine](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/architecture/formatting/index.md>) describes this part.
6. **Finish.** Trailing newlines are trimmed to one and line endings set by `newline_style`, as rustfmt's `format_lines` and `apply_newline_style` do.

For a file of 128 KiB or more, step 5 runs on several threads at once, one top-level item per task, while the text between items is written in order on one thread. [Parallelism and caches](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/architecture/concurrency/index.md>) covers that, and the caches that let chloro skip work it has done before.

## Where the time goes

On the 49-file instruction-count sample, after the performance work:

| part | share of instructions |
| --- | --- |
| lexing and parsing, including building the tree | 34% (42% on a crates.io sample) |
| the visitor and rewrites | most of the rest |
| memory allocation | about 12%, spread across both |

The parser is rust-analyzer's, used as published. Its remaining cost could be cut further only with a fork of `ra_ap_parser` (sizing its buffers up front and writing chloro's tree directly from its events), which would save at most about 6–7% of the total; chloro does not maintain a fork.

## The crates

| crate | what is in it |
| --- | --- |
| `chloro-core` | the lexer front end and flat tree (`cst`), the formatter (`formatter`), and the public entry points |
| `chloro` | the command line (`src/cli/`: argument parsing, file discovery, the worker pool, the caches) and a library facade over `chloro-core` |

`chloro-core`'s runtime dependency tree is 18 crates as `cargo tree` counts them (itself included), rust-analyzer's parser and its lexer among them; `syn` is not one of them. `rowan` and `ra_ap_syntax`, the tree types rust-analyzer itself uses, are only development dependencies: the tests use them to check that chloro builds the same tree as rust-analyzer.

# Parsing and the syntax tree

chloro parses with rust-analyzer's parser and stores the result as one flat array, so that reading a node of the tree is an array lookup that allocates nothing.

## Why rust-analyzer's parser

rustfmt parses with rustc's parser, which is only available inside the compiler. Of the parsers available as ordinary crates, rust-analyzer's (`ra_ap_parser`) is the one written to the same grammar and kept current with it, and it is lossless: every byte of the source, comments and whitespace included, belongs to a token in the tree. rustfmt depends on that information, because it recovers comments and blank lines by slicing the source between nodes.

The parser is used as published, pinned to one version (0.0.307 today) in `chloro-core/Cargo.toml`. It produces a stream of events (start node, token, finish node, error); chloro does everything after that, from building the tree to formatting.

## The lexer front end

rust-analyzer's own lexing step (`LexedStr`) restarts `rustc_lexer` at every token, converts each token kind, collects error messages, and then walks the tokens a second time to build the parser's input. chloro's `cst::lex` does both in one loop, into buffers sized from the text, and recognises the most common tokens (whitespace, ASCII identifiers, one-character punctuation, line comments) with a byte scan, handing the rest to `rustc_lexer`'s cursor.

It must produce exactly the tokens `LexedStr` produces, and two checks ensure that it does:

- Any text with a lexer error, a shebang or front matter goes to `LexedStr` as before, so error handling is rust-analyzer's own.
- `examples/lex_equality.rs` compares every token, every parser input call and the parser's output with `LexedStr`'s, over both corpora in two editions, 10,000 random texts and 10,000 mutated corpus files; and debug builds compare the two on every text they lex.

With this lexer, formatting the crates.io sample takes 15% fewer instructions.

## The flat tree

`cst::Tree` is the whole file as one `Vec` of 16-byte elements in preorder: each element is a node or a token, with its kind, its byte range in the source, and the index just past its subtree. Children are found by skipping subtrees; a token's text is a slice of the source, so no text is copied.

```text
     source: fn main() {}

index  kind              range   end
0      SOURCE_FILE       0..12   14
1        FN              0..12   14
2          FN_KW         0..2    3
3          WHITESPACE    2..3    4
4          NAME          3..7    6
5            IDENT       3..7    6
6          PARAM_LIST    7..9    9
7            L_PAREN     7..8    8
8            R_PAREN     8..9    9
9          WHITESPACE    9..10   10
10         BLOCK_EXPR    10..12  14
11           STMT_LIST   10..12  14
12             L_CURLY   10..11  13
13             R_CURLY   11..12  14
```

The tree of `fn main() {}`, as `cst::Tree::parse` builds it. `end` is the index after the element's subtree, so the next sibling of `NAME` (index 4) is at index 6.

A handle to a node or token (`Node`, `Token`) is a reference to the tree and an index. It is `Copy`, and making one allocates nothing. In `rowan`, the tree library rust-analyzer itself uses, reading a node creates a reference-counted "red" node on the heap. Replacing rowan's trees with this array cut the formatter's instructions by a quarter and its heap allocations by 43%.

On top of the array, a typed layer (`cst::ast`) has the same names as rust-analyzer's `ra_ap_syntax::ast`: `ast::Fn`, `expr.lhs()`, `item.name()`, `block.stmt_list()`. Its 501 accessors are generated from rust-analyzer's grammar file (`cst/rust.ungram`) by `cst/gen_ast.py`, and a test checks that the generated file is up to date.

The tree is built in one pass from the parser's events, attaching comments and whitespace to nodes by the rules rust-analyzer uses. Tests compare the result element by element with the tree rust-analyzer's own code builds through rowan, on every corpus file; debug builds make the same comparison on every tree they build.

## Macro arguments

rust-analyzer keeps the body of a macro call as an opaque token tree. rustfmt formats a call like `foo!(a + b, Vec<u8>)` by parsing each comma-separated argument as an expression, a type, a pattern or an item, in that order. chloro does the same with rust-analyzer's parser, and lays each argument's tree out at its original offset in the file, so spans, comments and source slices work inside macro arguments exactly as elsewhere. These fragment trees live in an arena that lasts for one formatting run.

## Where the two parsers disagree

rustfmt formats only what rustc's parser accepts, and leaves everything else alone. The two parsers accept almost the same syntax, with differences in both directions:

- **rust-analyzer accepts, rustc rejects.** rust-analyzer is deliberately permissive (it parses broken code in an editor) and accepts some removed or experimental syntax. `formatter/rustc_compat.rs` lists the rustc parse errors that matter, such as `<-` as an operator, `a..=` without an end, or misplaced doc comments, and returns such a file unchanged, as rustfmt would. Some of these rules depend on the rustfmt release being reproduced, because rustc 1.88's parser and rustc 1.97's differ.
- **rustc accepts, rust-analyzer rejects.** For a few constructs, such as a parenthesised first bound in a trait object (`Box<(Copy) + Send>`), a float literal used as a field name, or a `const` block as an item, `formatter/rustc_syntax.rs` rebuilds the tree with the node rustc would build, so the file is formatted as rustfmt formats it.

Two constructs remain where rust-analyzer's parser has no node to build; they are listed as [known differences](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/compatibility/#known-differences>).

# The formatting engine

chloro's formatter is a module-by-module port of rustfmt 1.9.0. An adaptation layer translates rust-analyzer's syntax tree for it, and a few additions make it faster without changing any formatting decision.

## Modules ported from rustfmt

The modules of `chloro-core/src/formatter/` carry the names of the rustfmt source files they reproduce, so a decision in chloro can be compared line by line with rustfmt's:

| module | role |
| --- | --- |
| `formatting` | the entry point: parse, visit, trailing newlines, newline style |
| `visitor`, `missed_spans` | walk items and statements; copy comments and blank lines between them |
| `items`, `imports`, `reorder` | items, `use` trees, the sorting of `use`, `mod` and `extern crate` |
| `expr`, `stmt`, `chains`, `closures`, `matches`, `pairs`, `patterns`, `types` | expressions and their parts |
| `macros`, `macro_args` | macro calls, with their arguments re-parsed, and `macro_rules!` bodies |
| `overflow`, `lists` | comma-separated lists and the "overflow the last item" heuristic |
| `attr`, `comment` | attributes, doc comments, re-indenting and recovering comments |
| `skip` | the names listed by `#[rustfmt::skip::macros(..)]` and `#[rustfmt::skip::attributes(..)]` |
| `shape`, `context`, `utils`, `sort` | shared infrastructure, as in rustfmt |

As in rustfmt, every node implements a `rewrite` method that takes a *shape* (the width available and the current indentation) and returns the node's text, or nothing if it cannot be laid out in that shape. A caller with several possible layouts tries them in rustfmt's order and keeps the first that succeeds: a call on one line, then with its last argument overflowing, then one argument per line, and so on.

Comments are handled as rustfmt handles them with its default (stable) options: re-indented and stripped of trailing whitespace, never re-wrapped.

## The adaptation layer

rustfmt is written against rustc's abstract syntax tree; chloro reads rust-analyzer's lossless tree. Three modules translate, so that the ported code can keep rustfmt's control flow:

- **`span`** computes rustc's spans. rustfmt recovers comments, blank lines and code it gives up on by slicing the source between nodes, so spans must start and end where rustc's do. The main difference is that rust-analyzer attaches leading comments to the following item, while a rustc span starts at the first attribute.
- **`nodes`** presents rust-analyzer's nodes in rustc's shape: doc comments as attributes, a block as a list of statements with its tail expression, rustc's classification of statements.
- **`macro_args`** parses macro call arguments as rustc's parser would (expression, then type, pattern or item), laying each argument's tree out at its offset in the file.

## Performance

rustfmt chooses a layout by rendering candidates and measuring them. Each attempt rewrites every subexpression again, so the work grows with nesting, exponentially in the worst case. chloro has to make the same choices, so it cannot skip an attempt that might succeed. It saves time by not repeating work and by skipping attempts that cannot succeed.

### A memo for deep nesting

A rewrite of an expression at a given shape is stored and reused when the same expression is asked for at the same shape again. On ordinary code that rarely happens (3.2% of lookups hit), and storing every result costs about as much as the hits save, so the memo only stores rewrites nested six or more deep (`MEMO_MIN_DEPTH`), where most repeated attempts happen. The memo is cleared at each top-level item.

### A lower bound on one-line width

Some attempts succeed only if their result fits on one line: a closure body without braces, or `if c { a } else { b }` on one line. `formatter/width.rs` computes, from a node's tokens and without rendering anything, a width below which no one-line rendering can be: the sum of the tokens that every formatting path writes unchanged (identifiers, keywords, literals, and the punctuation each node kind always writes). When the bound already exceeds the space available, the attempt is skipped, because it would fail.

The bound is justified token class by token class in the module's documentation, and tested against every actual one-line rendering over both corpora, three option sets and synthetic worst cases (`tests/width_bound.rs`). Its main effect is on deeply nested closures: a 2,000-byte file of closures nested 16 deep went from 105.4 million instructions to 5.7 million.

One case is also decided by structure alone: a closure body that renders a `match` with an arm is never one line. The argument for this comes from rustfmt's `rewrite_match`, and debug builds check it on every rewrite.

### Fewer, cheaper allocations

- Lists are written into the caller's buffer instead of being assembled and copied.
- Intermediate values that never leave one module (a call's list items, a chain's entries, a path's segments) live in a per-thread `bumpalo` arena, reset at each top-level item (`formatter/scratch.rs`), instead of being separate heap allocations. The arena uses no `unsafe` code.
- Dozens of local fast paths in the comment scanner, the list formatter and string building avoid re-scanning text, each tested against the computation it replaces. One of them is `chloro-core`'s only `unsafe` block: a 16-byte SSE2 load in the comment scanner, used only where the target supports it, with a randomised test against the scalar search.

None of these changes affects what a rewrite returns. Each was checked by formatting both corpora and comparing every file's output with the output recorded before the change.

## Modules not from rustfmt

- `width` and `scratch`, above.
- `parallel` and `unit_cache`: formatting top-level items on several threads, and reusing formatted items. See [Parallelism and caches](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/architecture/concurrency/index.md>).
- `rustc_compat` and `rustc_syntax`: the boundary between what rustc's parser and rust-analyzer's accept. See [Parsing](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/architecture/parsing/#where-the-two-parsers-disagree>).
- `printer`: a public `Printer` trait from chloro's pre-port formatter. Nothing in the formatter calls it; it is kept for API compatibility.

# Parallelism and caches

chloro can format parts of a file separately because, in rustfmt, the output of a top-level item depends only on that item, and the text between items can be filled in afterwards, in order.

## Item independence

rustfmt formats a file by walking its items in order with one visitor. Before building any parallelism, chloro tested whether each top-level item formats the same on its own as it does in its file. Splitting the rust-analyzer corpus and a crates.io corpus into units (one top-level item, or one group of `use`, `mod x;` or `extern crate` items that rustfmt sorts together) gave 13,650 units in the first and 965,193 in the second. Formatted on its own, every unit came out as it does in its file, except in the text before it: a comment before the item, a `#[rustfmt::skip]` module, a `#!` line. No unit differed in any other way.

So a unit's output depends only on its own text, the configuration, and the file's `rustfmt::skip::macros` and `::attributes` names. This was an empirical test rather than a proof, so both uses below are also tested for identical output over both corpora.

## Formatting items on several threads

`format_source_with_config_parallel` (`formatter/parallel.rs`) parses the file once into one immutable tree, which the threads share: a node handle is a reference and an index, and the tree is `Sync`. Workers take units from a shared queue, longest first, and each formats its unit with a visitor of its own, starting from the state the sequential visitor would have at that point.

The text before each unit needs special handling. The sequential visitor writes the comments and blank lines before an item from inside the item's own code, and what it writes depends on the output so far (whether the buffer is empty, how many newlines it ends with). A worker cannot know that, so it does not write the gap: it records the call it would have made. The calling thread then walks the units in order, replays each recorded gap call on the real output buffer, and appends the unit's text.

If a unit's record cannot be placed where it belongs, the calling thread formats that part sequentially instead; a panic in a worker is re-raised with its original payload. `tests/parallel_equivalence.rs` checks that the two paths give identical output, and the corpus check (`examples/bench --threads 4 --check`) compares the parallel output of every corpus file with hashes recorded from the sequential path.

## The command line's scheduler

The command line runs one worker per core and gives out files largest first from a shared queue. A file of 128 KiB or more is also split into items, on all threads; the file-level workers and the item-level threads share the cores, and the operating system schedules them. Measured with the `CHLORO_TRACE` timeline and rebuilt from per-thread CPU clocks, the resulting schedule is within 1–1.5% of the shortest the work allows, on every measured crate.

## The fixed-point cache

The command line's cache (`chloro/src/cli/cache.rs`) records one fact per entry: this exact file content, formatted by this binary under this configuration, comes out unchanged. It stores no formatted text, no paths and no timestamps. The binary and the configuration select the cache file; the content digests (BLAKE3, 256 bits) are its entries. The set is read once at start-up, shared read-only by the workers, and written once at the end through a temporary file and a rename. [Caching](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/guide/caching/index.md>) describes its behaviour and limits.

## The unit cache

`format_source_with_unit_cache` is the parallel function with a cache lookup before each unit is formatted. A cached unit records its output with every position relative to the unit's start, so a hit applies wherever the unit has moved in the file. Everything that depends on more than the unit is recomputed on every call: the parse, the whole-file checks, the text between units, and the final newline handling. A re-format after an edit to one item therefore costs a parse, one lookup per unit, and the edited unit.

The command line's `--unit-cache` stores these records in a file next to the fixed-point cache, keyed by the same binary and configuration. It was checked over both corpora, at one and four threads, to give output identical to formatting without it.

# Optional

# Development

How the repository is laid out, how to build and test it, and the checks a change must pass. A change that alters any formatted output is a conformance change and must say so; any other change must leave every output byte unchanged.

## Layout

| path | what is there |
| --- | --- |
| `chloro-core/src/cst/` | the lexer front end (`lex.rs`), the flat syntax tree (`mod.rs`), and the typed layer (`ast.rs`, `generated.rs` from `gen_ast.py` and `rust.ungram`) |
| `chloro-core/src/formatter/` | the ported rustfmt modules, the adaptation layer, `parallel.rs`, `unit_cache.rs`, `width.rs` |
| `chloro-core/tests/` | unit and integration tests, and the conformance suite under `tests/conformance/` |
| `chloro-core/examples/` | the measurement and comparison tools (`conform`, `config_matrix`, `bench`, `lex_equality`, `unit_cache`, …) |
| `chloro/src/cli/` | the command line: arguments, file discovery, the worker pool, the caches, the trace |
| `benchmarks/` | the benchmark harness against rustfmt, the instruction-count profiler, the PGO build script |
| `docs/site/` | this website's sources; `zensical.toml` at the root configures it |
| `docs/journal/` | the development journal: design records, experiments and measurements, in the format of `docs/JOURNAL.md` |

## Building and testing

```sh
cargo build --workspace --all-features
cargo test --workspace --all-features
```

`--all-features` includes the measurement-only allocator features (`alloc-jemalloc` and the others), which need a C toolchain; jemalloc does not build with MSVC, so on Windows test with `--features chloro/cli` instead, in a checkout made with `core.autocrlf` off: the tests compare fixtures, snapshots and generated code byte for byte.

The `Justfile` wraps the usual commands: `just test` (with `cargo nextest`), `just clippy` (`-D warnings`, all targets and features), `just check`, `just docs` (rustdoc). Formatting and lint hooks run through [prek](<https://github.com/j178/prek>) or pre-commit: `just install-hooks`, then `just precommit`. Commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](<https://www.conventionalcommits.org/>), enforced by a `commit-msg` hook, because the release tooling builds the changelog from them.

`README.md` and `chloro/README.md` are kept identical (`just docs-match` checks; `just docs-mirror` copies the newer over the older): the second is the README crates.io shows for `chloro`.

## Conformance

The conformance suite lives in `chloro-core/tests/conformance/`:

- `fixtures/rust-analyzer/` holds 1238 `.rs` files from rust-analyzer, the corpus.
- `snapshots/ra/<crate>/<case>.rustfmt.rs` holds rustfmt 1.9.0's output for each, or the input itself where rustfmt rejects the file. `snapshots/ra-1.8.0/` holds rustfmt 1.8.0's output where it differs from 1.9.0's.
- `rustfmt-versions/` holds a reproducer for each class of difference between rustfmt 1.8.0 and 1.9.0.

`conform` compares chloro with the stored snapshots, without running rustfmt:

```sh
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example conform -- -i            # 1.9.0
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example conform -- -i -V 1.8.0   # 1.8.0
```

It reports the number of identical files, diff totals, files that are not idempotent (`-i`), and throughput. The batch test regenerates the snapshots with the `rustfmt` on `PATH`, and writes chloro's output and a diff beside each:

```sh
cargo test -p chloro-core --test conformance batch
```

For the `parser` and `syntax` crates (581 small cases) only the `.rustfmt.rs` files are tracked; the outputs and diffs are written locally and ignored by git. `just conf` summarises the current diffs, and `just conf-plain` prints the summary without colour.

`config_matrix` compares option values and other corpora against a live rustfmt:

```sh
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example config_matrix -- -n 1220
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example config_matrix -- --root ~/.cargo/registry/src -n 30000 default
```

The registry corpus is the 577 crates named in `docs/journal/2026-10-14-autoresearch/corpus/registry-manifest.toml`, fetched into the cargo registry.

## Checks for a change

CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) runs on every pull request: `cargo fmt --check`, clippy with warnings denied, the tests on Linux, macOS (arm64) and Windows, a build of the `aarch64-pc-windows-msvc` release target, `cargo check` on Rust 1.88 (the workspace's `rust-version`), and `conform -i` at both rustfmt releases. The arm64 runner matters: the byte search in `formatter/comment.rs` has an SSE2 path on x86-64 and a portable one elsewhere.

A change that is meant to leave the output alone (a performance change, a refactor) must show that it does. In order, cheapest first:

1. `cargo fmt --check`, `just clippy`, `cargo test --workspace --all-features`.
2. **Output hashes.** Record the hash of every corpus file's output before the change, and check them after:

   ```sh
   cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example bench -- --record before.tsv   # on the base
   cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example bench -- --check before.tsv    # on the change
   cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example bench -- --threads 4 --check before.tsv
   ```

   Zero files may change, sequentially or with four threads. Add `--root ~/.cargo/registry/src` to do the same over the registry corpus.
3. `conform -i` at both rustfmt releases: no fewer identical files, none non-idempotent.
4. `config_matrix -n 1220`: no option value loses a file.
5. For a performance claim, the instruction count on both samples ([Benchmarking](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/maintainers/benchmarking/index.md>)).

A conformance fix changes outputs on purpose: the files it changes should be exactly the ones it targets, checked file by file, and the case recorded in the conformance ledger.

## Code conventions

- **rustfmt's structure.** Formatter modules keep rustfmt's module, function and variable names and its control flow, so that a difference can be traced to the rustfmt code it reproduces. Optimisations are written so that this correspondence stays readable.
- **Public API.** Changes are additive: `format_source` and `format_source_with_config` keep their signatures, and new capabilities are new functions.
- **`unsafe` code.** `chloro` forbids it. `chloro-core` has one `unsafe` block, with a written safety argument and a randomised test. Any new one needs the same, and a safe alternative measured first.
- **Dependencies.** A new dependency needs a measured reason. `chloro-core` has 18 crates in its runtime tree.

## The journal

`docs/journal/` records design decisions, experiments and measurements as dated entries, in the format `docs/JOURNAL.md` describes. The journal records why things are the way they are; this website describes how chloro works now. The [project history](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/history/index.md>) is a guide to the journal.

# Upgrading the parser

chloro reimplements two pieces of rust-analyzer's parser crate for speed: its lexing step and its tree building. Both are pinned to the behaviour of one `ra_ap_parser` release, so after a version bump they must be checked against the new release.

## What is pinned

| dependency | version | why chloro depends on its exact behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ra_ap_parser` | 0.0.307 | the grammar; `cst::lex` reproduces its `LexedStr::new` and `to_input`, and `TreeBuilder::steps_fused` reproduces its `intersperse_trivia` |
| `ra-ap-rustc_lexer` | 0.137.0 | the tokeniser `cst::lex` drives directly, the same version `ra_ap_parser` uses |
| `rustc-literal-escaper` | 0.0.4 | literal validation, as in `LexedStr` |
| `ra_ap_syntax`, `rowan` (dev) | 0.0.307, 0.15.15 | the reference the equality tests compare chloro's tree with |
| `cst/rust.ungram` | copied from the `ra_ap_syntax` 0.0.307 crate | the grammar the typed layer is generated from |

The three runtime crates are upgraded together: `ra-ap-rustc_lexer` and `rustc-literal-escaper` are the versions `ra_ap_parser` itself depends on.

## The equality harnesses

Each reimplementation has a harness that compares it with the code it replaces. Release builds do not run these comparisons; debug builds also run them inline, on every input.

| what | harness | what it compares |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the lexer front end (`cst/lex.rs`) | `examples/lex_equality.rs` | every token's kind and offset, every call that builds the parser's input, and the parser's output, against `LexedStr` and `to_input`; over the corpus in editions 2021 and 2024, 10,000 random texts and 10,000 mutated corpus files in all four editions |
| the lexer front end, inline | debug builds of `cst::lex` | the same comparison on every text a debug build lexes |
| the fused tree build (`TreeBuilder::steps_fused`) | `cst` tests `fused_build_equals_the_interspersed_build*` | the fused build against the build through rust-analyzer's `intersperse_trivia`, on sample sources and every corpus file |
| the flat tree as a whole | `cst` tests `flat_tree_equals_the_rowan_tree*` | chloro's tree against the rowan tree `ra_ap_syntax` builds, node by node |
| the fused build, inline | debug builds of `TreeBuilder::steps` | the fused build against `intersperse_trivia` on every tree a debug build makes |
| the typed layer | `cst::ast` test `generated_layer_is_up_to_date` | the checked-in `generated.rs` against `gen_ast.py`'s output |

## Bumping `ra_ap_parser`

1. **Bump the versions together.** In `chloro-core/Cargo.toml`, set `ra_ap_parser` and the development dependencies `ra_ap_syntax` and `rowan` to the new release's versions, and `ra-ap-rustc_lexer` and `rustc-literal-escaper` to the versions the new `ra_ap_parser` depends on (`cargo tree -p ra_ap_parser`).
2. **Regenerate the typed layer.** Copy `rust.ungram` from the root of the new `ra_ap_syntax` crate (in the cargo registry once the dependency is fetched) over `chloro-core/src/cst/rust.ungram`, and run the generator, passing `ra_ap_syntax`'s own generated nodes so the script checks that the accessor set matches:

   ```sh
   python3 chloro-core/src/cst/gen_ast.py chloro-core/src/cst/rust.ungram \
       chloro-core/src/cst/generated.rs \
       ~/.cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-*/ra_ap_syntax-<version>/src/ast/generated/nodes.rs
   ```

   It prints any difference and exits with 1 if there is one.
3. **Read the diffs of the reimplemented code.** In the new `ra_ap_parser`, compare `lexed_str.rs` (`LexedStr::new`), `shortcuts.rs` (`to_input`, `intersperse_trivia`) and the trivia attachment rules with the previous release. A change there needs the same change in `cst/lex.rs` or `cst/mod.rs`; the module documentation of each names the source it follows.
4. **Run the harnesses.**

   ```sh
   cargo test -p chloro-core --lib cst                         # tree equality, generated layer
   cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example lex_equality   # 0 mismatches required
   cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example lex_equality -- --root ~/.cargo/registry/src
   cargo run -p chloro-core --example bench -- -n 1            # debug build: every inline check, on the corpus
   ```

   Each prints its mismatches and exits with 1 if there is any. The debug `bench` run is slow; it is the one that exercises the inline checks on every file.
5. **Run the conformance checks.** A parser change can change what parses. Record output hashes on the old version, then compare on the new one, and rerun `conform` and `config_matrix` as in [Development](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/maintainers/development/#checks-for-a-change>). Any output that changes needs to be explained by a change in rust-analyzer's grammar, and compared with rustfmt.
6. **Check the rustc boundary.** `formatter/rustc_compat.rs` and `formatter/rustc_syntax.rs` encode where rust-analyzer's parser and rustc's disagree. A new release may close a gap (a `rustc_syntax` rebuild is no longer needed) or open one; the conformance ledger lists the cases each rule covers.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Release builds do not check**
>
> The inline comparisons run only in debug builds. A release build on a new parser version that skipped step 4 would silently produce whatever the stale reimplementation produces.

# Benchmarking

chloro's performance work uses two kinds of measurement: instruction counts, which are repeatable on any machine, and wall-time comparisons with rustfmt, which need an idle machine and are compared only as ratios.

The scripts are in `benchmarks/`; `benchmarks/README.md` documents every option. They need a release build of both crates first:

```sh
cargo build --release -p chloro --features cli
cargo build --release -p chloro-core --examples
```

## Instruction counts: `profile.sh`

```sh
benchmarks/profile.sh --core 3
benchmarks/profile.sh --core 3 --sample-list benchmarks/samples/registry49.txt
benchmarks/profile.sh --core 3 --runs 3 --per-file
benchmarks/profile.sh --core 3 --runs 3 --per-file --phase parse
```

`profile.sh` runs the CLI under valgrind's callgrind and reports the instructions executed (`Ir`). Two samples of 49 files are used, and a change is judged on both:

- the **fixture sample**, every 25th file of the conformance corpus (650 KB);
- the **registry sample**, 49 files from tokio, regex-syntax, clap\_builder and winnow (`benchmarks/samples/registry49.txt`, 732 KB), so that a change tuned on one sample is checked on code it was not tuned on.

Counts repeat to within about 2,000 instructions from run to run, so changes far below timing noise are visible. The script does two things to keep the counts stable:

- The script stages the binary and the sample under fixed-length paths and runs with address randomisation off (`setarch -R`) and an empty environment, because path lengths shift the heap's layout and with it the count.
- `--per-file` formats each file in its own process and sums the counts, which removes the effect one file's allocations have on the next file's. A change of less than about 2 million instructions is judged on the per-file figure.

`--phase parse` counts only the parse (`chloro_core::parse_only`), to see the parser's share. `--sim` adds callgrind's cache and branch simulation; `--shuffle N` repeats the count with randomised code layouts, to tell a real change from an effect of code layout.

Needs `valgrind` and `setarch`.

## Against rustfmt: `compare_rustfmt.sh`

```sh
benchmarks/compare_rustfmt.sh --list                              # the workloads
benchmarks/compare_rustfmt.sh -r 15 -w 2 --rounds 2 --core 3      # the full comparison
benchmarks/compare_rustfmt.sh -r 5 --rounds 2 fx-hir fx-hir-ty    # some workloads
python3 benchmarks/report.py benchmarks/results/<stamp>           # tables from a run
```

The script times rustfmt and chloro with hyperfine on the same files: nine crates (five from rust-analyzer, four from crates.io), 287 small files, a 13-byte file for start-up, single large files through standard input, and in-process runs. For each workload it holds equal:

- **the bytes:** both tools read copies of the same files, by default formatted by rustfmt first, because rustfmt's `--check` builds a diff of every file that would change;
- **the file set:** taken from rustfmt's own list of the files it formats, then verified;
- **the configuration:** defaults for both, with an empty config file for rustfmt;
- **the order:** the command order is reversed in alternate rounds;
- **the output:** before timing, each command runs once and must succeed; whether the two outputs agree is recorded per workload.

It records wall time, CPU time and peak memory for each run under `benchmarks/results/<UTC stamp>/`, and `report.py` turns that into tables. Pinned rows (`--core`) put both tools on one core; unpinned rows let chloro use every core.

Needs `hyperfine` 2.0, `taskset`, `jq`, `python3`, and rustfmt 1.9.0 (the script resolves the real binary behind rustup's proxy).

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Wall time on a shared machine**
>
> Timings of the same binary on the same files varied by 20–40% between measurement sessions on the virtual machine chloro was measured on. Compare tools within one run, never across runs, and treat a wall-time change smaller than the run-to-run spread as no change.

## On any Cargo project: `just vs-rustfmt`

```sh
just vs-rustfmt path/to/project      # chloro, chloro --threads 1 and cargo fmt
just vs-ruff                         # the same on ruff, in ~/tmp/ruff (cloned if missing)
just vs-ruff ~/src/ruff 10           # another checkout, 10 runs
```

These recipes (`.just/bench.just`) give both tools the same files: the list `cargo fmt --all` formats, so each file is formatted once. A plain `rustfmt` over every `.rs` file of a project formats each module file several times, because rustfmt also formats the modules a file declares; on ruff that is 3.6 passes per file. Both tools run in check mode, so use an already-formatted tree. They need `hyperfine`.

They time the `chloro` on your `PATH`, first making sure it was built from this checkout. `just reinstall` installs the CLI with a build ID baked in, which `chloro --version` prints (`chloro 0.9.0-dev (2f9b060, build <id>)`); `just build-id` computes the ID of the checkout as it is on disk, from the content of every file that goes into the binary (committed or not), `Cargo.lock`, the toolchain and the install command. When the two match, the benchmark starts at once without running Cargo; when they differ, or the installed `chloro` has no build ID, the recipe runs `just reinstall` first, outside the timed runs.

## In process: `bench`

```sh
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example bench -- -n 5                # MB/s on the corpus
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example bench -- --root ~/.cargo/registry/src
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example bench -- --phase parse       # the parse alone
```

`bench` times `format_source` over every file, excluding I/O and process start-up, and reports the best of `-n` rounds. It also records and checks output hashes ([Development](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/maintainers/development/#checks-for-a-change>)).

## Other tools

| tool | what it is for |
| --- | --- |
| `benchmarks/cliffs/` | synthetic inputs of 20 shapes at growing sizes, fitted for how instruction counts scale, to find inputs where the work grows faster than the input |
| `benchmarks/schedule/` | turning a `CHLORO_TRACE` timeline into per-worker idle time, and rebuilding the schedule from CPU clocks |
| `examples/alloc_count.rs` | counting allocations |
| `alloc-timing`, `alloc-mimalloc`, `alloc-jemalloc`, `alloc-snmalloc` features | instrumenting or replacing the global allocator in measurement builds; all off by default |

## Measurement records

Six full measurements against rustfmt (M1 to M6) and the experiments behind each change are in the journal; the [project history](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/history/index.md>) explains how to find them. The [Performance](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/performance/index.md>) page summarises the latest.

# Releasing

chloro is released with release-plz from the master branch. Both crates are released together at the same version, each gets a tag and a GitHub release, and publishing the `chloro` release builds the binaries.

## Release process

```sh
just ship            # release-plz picks the version from the commits
just ship 0.9.0      # or set it
```

`just ship` refuses to run unless master is checked out, clean and up to date with `origin/master`. It then:

1. dry-runs the publish (`release-plz release --dry-run`);
2. runs `just prepush` (check, clippy, rustdoc) and `just precommit` (formatting, lints, the README badges) on the tree as it is, and stops if either fails or changes a file, before anything is modified;
3. bumps the versions of `chloro` and `chloro-core` (`release-plz set-version`, or `release-plz update` to pick the version from the commits), checks that `CHANGELOG.md` has a section for the new version, and commits the bump; a failure in this step resets the tree to where it started;
4. pushes, and runs `release-plz release`, which publishes both crates to crates.io and creates the tags (`chloro-v<version>`, `chloro-core-v<version>`) and GitHub releases;
5. sets both releases' notes from the version's section of `CHANGELOG.md` (`just release-notes-publish <version>`; `just release-notes <version>` prints them).

The root `CHANGELOG.md` is the only changelog: release-plz does not update the per-crate ones (`changelog_update = false`), which end at 0.7.5. Its `set-version` used to rename their newest heading instead of adding an entry, which gave 0.8.0 and 0.9.0 the 0.7.5 notes.

`just ship-manual` is a fallback for when release-plz is not working.

## Before a release

CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) runs on every pull request and push to master: formatting, clippy, the tests on Linux, macOS (arm64) and Windows, a build of the Windows arm64 target, `cargo check` on the minimum Rust version, and `conform -i` at both rustfmt releases.

- \[ \] CI is green on the commit to be released.
- \[ \] `config_matrix -n 1220` (against a live rustfmt, so not in CI) is identical on every value ([Development](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/maintainers/development/#conformance>)).
- \[ \] If `ra_ap_parser` changed since the last release, the [parser harnesses](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/maintainers/parser-upgrades/index.md>) were run.
- \[ \] The root `CHANGELOG.md`: move the *Unreleased* entries under the new version and date. `just ship` stops if the section is missing, and the release notes are taken from it.
- \[ \] The README badges (dependency count, binary size) are current: `just emblazon`.
- \[ \] `README.md` and `chloro/README.md` are identical (`just docs-match`); the second is what crates.io shows.
- \[ \] The website's [Installation](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/getting-started/installation/index.md>) note about unreleased features, and the release named there, are updated.

## Binaries

Publishing the GitHub release for a `chloro-v*` tag runs `.github/workflows/binaries.yml`, which builds the CLI for each target and attaches the archives to the release (`chloro-core-v*` releases have none). Their names match the `[package.metadata.binstall]` section of `chloro/Cargo.toml`, which is how `cargo binstall chloro` finds them.

| target | runner | build |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` | `ubuntu-22.04` | profile-guided |
| `x86_64-apple-darwin` | `macos-latest` (arm64) | plain (cross-compiled) |
| `aarch64-apple-darwin` | `macos-latest` (arm64) | profile-guided |
| `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` | `windows-2022` | profile-guided, static CRT |
| `aarch64-pc-windows-msvc` | `windows-2022` | plain (cross-compiled), static CRT |

A target that fails does not stop the others, and fails the run. The 0.8.0 and 0.9.0 releases have no macOS archives (their jobs waited for the retired `macos-13` runner until cancelled), and 0.9.0 none for `aarch64-pc-windows-msvc` (an `unused_mut` warning on non-x86 targets, made an error by `-D warnings`, which release builds no longer set).

The workflow can be run by hand for an existing tag, from the Actions tab or with `gh workflow run binaries.yml -f tag=chloro-v0.9.0`. By default it is a dry run, which builds and archives every target and uploads nothing; with `-f dry-run=false` it uploads the archives to that tag's release, replacing any of the same name, so name the missing targets with `-f targets="x86_64-apple-darwin aarch64-apple-darwin"`. The build checks out the tag, so `chloro --version` prints the release's plain version.

### Profile-guided builds

`benchmarks/pgo.sh` builds chloro with profile-guided optimisation: it compiles an instrumented binary (`-Cprofile-generate`), runs it over the conformance corpus with `--check` and through `bench`, merges the profile with `llvm-profdata` (from the `llvm-tools-preview` component), and builds again with `-Cprofile-use`.

```sh
benchmarks/pgo.sh                                  # local profile-guided build
benchmarks/pgo.sh --phase train --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
benchmarks/pgo.sh --phase use --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
```

The release workflow runs the training phase on each target whose runner executes it natively and sets `RUSTFLAGS` so the upload step's build uses the profile. A cross-compiled target, or one whose training fails, gets the plain build with a warning in the log. On the measurements, the profile-guided build executed 16% fewer instructions than the plain one and ran in 0.80–0.95 of its wall time, with identical output.

0.9.0 was the first release built this way: the `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` job trained a 1.09 MB profile and built with it, with no `no profile data available` warnings. On later releases, read each target's log for `PGO skipped`, `PGO training failed` and those warnings.

## Versions

Both crates share a version (0.9.0 at the latest release). `chloro` depends on `chloro-core` at the same version through the workspace's `[workspace.dependencies]`. The minimum supported Rust version is the workspace's `rust-version`, 1.88.

# Documentation

Where chloro's documentation lives, and how this website is built, checked and published to GitHub Pages.

## Where documentation lives

| where | for | source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| this website, [https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/>) | using and maintaining chloro: guides, compatibility, performance, architecture | `docs/site/`, `zensical.toml` |
| [docs.rs/chloro](<https://docs.rs/chloro>), [docs.rs/chloro-core](<https://docs.rs/chloro-core>) | the Rust API, item by item | doc comments in the code |
| `README.md` | a first look on GitHub and crates.io, with links here | `README.md`, mirrored to `chloro/README.md` |
| `CHANGELOG.md` | what changed in each release, for users; shown on the [Changelog](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/changelog/index.md>) page | `CHANGELOG.md` |
| `docs/journal/` | the record of decisions, experiments and measurements | dated Markdown entries, see the [project history](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/history/index.md>) |

Each fact should be documented in one place. The website describes what chloro does and links to the journal for the evidence, rather than copying experiment records.

## Building the site

The site is built with [Zensical](<https://zensical.org>), as the documentation of [nave](<https://lmmx.github.io/nave/>) is. It needs only [uv](<https://docs.astral.sh/uv/>):

```sh
just site-serve        # live preview at http://localhost:8000/chloro/
just site-build        # build into site/ (ignored by git)
```

The recipes pin Zensical's version (`ZENSICAL` in `.just/site.just`), and the deployment workflow pins the same one. To upgrade, change both and check the site.

## Checks

```sh
just site-check        # nav, links and the CLI help snippet
just site-examples     # compile and run every Rust example
```

- `site-check` builds the site, then runs `docs/scripts/check_site.py`: every page is in the nav and every nav entry exists; every internal link, image and stylesheet of the built site resolves, anchors included, under the `/chloro/` base path the site is served from; and `docs/site/_snippets/cli/help.txt` matches the current `chloro --help`. Zensical's own build also reports links to missing pages and anchors.
- `site-examples` runs `docs/scripts/check_examples.py`, which turns every fenced `rust` block under `docs/site/` into a test of a scratch crate (in `target/docs-examples/`) that depends on the workspace's crates, and runs them. A block is the body of a test function, as in a doctest, so it can declare items and `assert!` its results.

When the CLI's help text changes, `just site-snippets` regenerates the snippet that the [CLI reference](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-110/reference/cli/index.md>) includes.

## Writing pages

- Pages are Markdown with the extensions configured in `zensical.toml`: admonitions (`!!! note`), tabs (`=== "Title"`), collapsible blocks (`??? info`), definition lists, footnotes, and keys (`++"--check"++` renders a flag as a key cap). `--8<-- "path"` includes a file, relative to the repository root.
- Add a new page to the `nav` in `zensical.toml`; `site-check` fails on a page that is not in it.
- Give each page a front-matter `description` (one sentence, at most 160 characters), and list the page with the same description in the `llmstxt` sections of `zensical.toml`. The description is the page's meta description for search engines and its entry in `llms.txt`; `site-check` fails on a page without one, or one listed with another.
- Link between pages with relative paths to the `.md` files. Link to the journal, the source and anything else in the repository with absolute GitHub URLs on `master`, since those files are not part of the site.
- State measured figures with their conditions, and link to the record they come from.

## For agents and LLMs

Zensical's built-in `llmstxt` plugin, configured in `zensical.toml`, adds to every build:

- `llms.txt`, an index of the pages in the [llms.txt](<https://llmstxt.org/>) format, with each page's description; the maintainers' pages are under *Optional*;
- `llms-full.txt`, every listed page in one file;
- a Markdown copy of each page beside its HTML, `<page>/index.md`, converted from the built page (snippets included, links absolute);
- `<link rel="alternate" type="text/markdown">` and `<link rel="describedby">` (to `llms.txt`) in each page's head.

Each page also has a *Copy as Markdown* button (`content.action.copy`). `AGENTS.md` at the repository root is the entry point for coding agents working on the code, and the README links all of these.

GitHub Pages serves the site from a subpath, so a `robots.txt` (which must be at the domain root) is not possible, and it cannot negotiate content or set headers: an agent asking for `text/markdown` gets HTML, and finds the Markdown through the links above. The sitemap is at `sitemap.xml`.

## Design

The site follows the design of nave's documentation: Zensical's modern theme, Instrument Serif for page titles, Encode Sans Condensed for headings, Work Sans for text, commands set as key caps. chloro's own colours are chlorophyll greens, defined as CSS variables for the light and dark schemes in `docs/site/assets/stylesheets/extra.css`, with a toggle in the header. The mark is a seedling whose big leaf has veins that branch like a syntax tree, in `docs/site/assets/images/`: `chloro-hero.svg` and `chloro-hero-dark.svg` on the home page, with a ground shadow, sheen and highlights drawn with gradients (no filters); `chloro-small.svg` and `chloro-small-dark.svg` (flat, without veins) in the header; and `chloro.svg`, the favicon, which switches to the dark palette when the browser prefers dark. Charts and diagrams are inline SVG drawn with the page's colour variables, so they follow the scheme, and each chart has its data in a table beside it.

## Deployment

GitHub Pages serves the site from the `gh-pages` branch (Settings → Pages → Build and deployment → Source: *Deploy from a branch*, `gh-pages`, `/ (root)`). `.github/workflows/site.yml` writes to that branch:

- **Production.** Every push to `master` builds the site and deploys it to the root of `gh-pages`, which is served at [https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/](<https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/>). The deploy replaces everything at the root except the `pr-preview/` directory.
- **Pull request previews.** A pull request that changes the site (`docs/site/`, `zensical.toml`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `docs/scripts/` or the workflow) is built with its `site_url` set to its preview path and deployed to `gh-pages/pr-preview/pr-<number>/`, served at `https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-<number>/`. The workflow posts the link as a comment on the pull request once GitHub Pages has published it, edits that same comment on later pushes, and deletes the preview when the pull request is closed or merged.

Every pull request also runs the build and `docs/scripts/check_site.py`, whether or not it gets a preview. Pull requests from forks get the checks but no preview: their workflows have a read-only token and cannot push to `gh-pages`. The job that deploys a preview checks out the default branch, not the pull request, and publishes only the files the build job produced.

The production and preview deploys write to separate paths of the branch, and each rebases and retries if the branch moved while it ran, so they can run at the same time. The `gh-pages` branch keeps every deploy as a commit.

The workflow reads the Pages source at the start of each run. While the source is still *GitHub Actions*, it also publishes `master` with `actions/deploy-pages` and does not deploy previews; once the source is the `gh-pages` branch, that job is skipped. The workflow can also be run by hand from the Actions tab.

# Project history

chloro keeps a development journal: dated records of what was decided, what was measured, and what was tried and did not work. This page explains how the journal is organised and where to start reading it.

The journal is the [`docs/journal/`](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/tree/master/docs/journal>) directory of the repository. Entries are Markdown files named `YYYY-MM-DD-title.md`, written to the format in [`docs/JOURNAL.md`](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/JOURNAL.md>): statements of what exists, with the files and figures that support them, and no recommendations.

## Timeline

| when | what happened | entries |
| --- | --- | --- |
| November–December 2025 | 0.5 to 0.7: a hand-written formatter over rust-analyzer's `rowan` trees, matching rustfmt on 233 of 1220 conformance files | the per-crate changelogs |
| 9–11 October 2026 | The rustfmt port: rustfmt 1.9.0's formatting logic ported module by module onto rust-analyzer's syntax trees, reaching 1219 of 1220. Then an investigation of where the port's time goes, and whether the proof of concept was a better foundation. It was not: most of its speed came from work it skipped. Released as 0.8.0. | [rustfmt port](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-09-rustfmt-port.md>), [performance checkpoint](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-10-performance-checkpoint.md>), [change of direction](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-10-change-of-direction.md>), [item independence](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-10-item-independence.md>), [representations](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-10-representations.md>), [phase 2 close](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-11-phase-2-close.md>) |
| 14–17 October 2026 | The performance and conformance programme: 31 experiments run in parallel on separate branches, each kept only if it passed every check twice and changed no output it was not meant to change; six full measurements against rustfmt on an idle machine. It reached 1220 of 1220, added rustfmt 1.8.0 support, and cut instructions by 66%. | [programme](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-14-autoresearch.md>), [handoff](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-17-handoff.md>) |
| 17 October 2026 | The documentation site, `chloro --version` with a development-build marker, a benchmark recipe for any Cargo project, and a measurement on ruff. Released, with the programme above, as 0.9.0. | [release](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-17-release-0.9.0.md>) |

## Reading the performance programme

The programme's records use short codes. Start with the [handoff](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-17-handoff.md>), which is written for a reader who did not follow the work: it explains every code and summarises each experiment, failure and measurement with its source.

| code | meaning | where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E1 … E31 | experiments, one hypothesis each, with a written record | [ledger](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-14-autoresearch/experiments.md>), `experiments/EXP-NNN-*.md` |
| R2, R5 | the conformance fixes, and the fixes for a code review's findings | [conformance ledger](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-14-autoresearch/conformance-ledger.md>) |
| M1 … M6 | the six full measurements against rustfmt on an idle machine | [measurements](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/tree/master/docs/journal/2026-10-14-autoresearch/measurements>) |
| P1 … P11 | the ranked list of parser-side improvements | [parser theory record](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-15-extensions-theory/parser-and-substrate.md>) |
| "base", "the start" | `884f9c9`, release 0.8.0 |  |
| "best-known-good" | the latest commit whose checks were reproduced on the merged branch | [ledger](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-14-autoresearch/experiments.md>) |
| `Ir` | instructions executed, as counted by callgrind |  |

Other records that are useful on their own:

- The [protocol](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-14-autoresearch/protocol.md>): what counts as a result, the checks a change must pass, and how work on an approach is stopped.
- The [conformance ledger](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-14-autoresearch/conformance-ledger.md>): every mismatch with rustfmt found, its root cause, and the six cases still open.
- The [rustfmt versions record](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-14-autoresearch/rustfmt-versions.md>): where rustfmt 1.7.0, 1.8.0 and 1.9.0 differ on real code, and why 1.7.0 is not supported.
- The records of approaches that did not improve performance, each with the measurement that ruled it out: a faster allocator, code layout, a resident server process, scheduling, an exact width model. The handoff's sections 7 and 12 list them.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Commit hashes in the journal**
>
> The commits of the performance branch were re-recorded under the maintainer's name before the branch was merged, which gave them new hashes. The journal's references read `new` (was `old`): the commit's hash in the repository, with the hash recorded at the time beside it. Commands, file names and tool output quoted in the records keep the original hashes; [2026-10-17-commit-map.md](<https://github.com/lmmx/chloro/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-17-commit-map.md>) maps every one of them.
